Tea ei lei Sir Andrew Clarke, For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pore. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated.

It is very satisfactory to them' that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital: . _ •

"Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, allot one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock. when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me : ' Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of 'ea.' I Bay 'thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like It strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody. and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful In its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, BO disorders the inrvous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooisful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." - • -• • - -•- • • •
Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned ea is like.

The colour of the tea after it is breted will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable tor the system, unit if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
" YEs," said Conservative Goggs, "I never like change—except when it is in my pocket." MONEY and time are valuable; but a man may be miserable with both when he has more of either
_ than he can- spend. CARL—" Mother, in the milk bucket a dead mouse was." Mother—" Well, hast thou it the:emit taken ?" Carl—" No: I have the cat

therein throvn." IT is a pretty healthy man who can reada patent medicine almanac without suddenly discovering that he .is afflicted with about 150 of the 200 diseases described therein. " WHAT station do you call this?" asked a man as he crawled out of the ruins of a carriage after a went railroad accident. "Devastation, sir," refolied his fellow-passengers in chorus. TuE town-crier of Kilkenny took in charge a lost child, and proceeded to hunt up its owners. On being asked by a lady what was the matter, he .re- plied, "Here's an orphan child, ma'am, and I'm trying to find its parents." CLERS. (to employer) : "What shall I mark that new lot of black silk at Employer: "Mark the selling price $3 a yard." Clerk: "But it only cost $1 a yard." Employer: "I don't care what it cost. I am selling off regardless of cost."—American Paper. THE patron of a cheap eating-house, who com- plained that they now gave him one potato with his meat, wh'ereas they formerly gave him two, was mollified by the waiter's explanation—that the last lot of ;potatoes they purchased was so bad that no gentleman could eat more than one of them. IN an old-fashioned meeting-house in which the men and women were seated apart, the clergyman, interrupted by loud talking, stopped short in his sermon. A woman, speaking for, her sex, said. "Your reverence, the noise is not among us," "So much the better," said the minister; "it will

be the sooner over." "I REMEMBER," says Lord Eldon, "Mr. .Tustice Gould trying a case at York, and when he had proceeded for about two hours, he observed: "Here are only eleven jurymen in the box; where is the twelfth?" "Please you, my Lord," said one of the eleven, "he has gone away about some business, but he has left his verdict with me." "HAVE you got a hair dye of your own?" he asked of the barber as the shears clipped off the grey looks. "I have sir." "Do you warrant it?" "I do." "To do what?" "To make your wife so jealous of yun inside of six weeks that she'll.put a private detective on your track." The old man maid "11'm ? " and the subject was dropped. "DAN," said a nouveau riche earnestly to his eldest son, "you must be more careful when you get in any more wine?" "Which wine do you mean!" inquired Dan. "The claret. I heard one of your swell friends tell his neighbour at dessert last night that the claret was very old. Get it fresh, Dan, no matter what it costa

" Well,' replied the honest old believer, with meaning emphasis, "I don't see why it ain't as easy for an asstotalklikeamanasitisfori. map to talk like an ass.". A aii..l-WhO fee6tly invested in some sausages says that when he got them home he cut them apart and left them. In the morning he visited them. Three of them were twined up together and were sleeping siyeetiy. TIVq kasl cralyled the milk bowl and were lalying the milk, and one, a black and white one, was on the garden wall trying to catch a sparrow. He drowned the lot. CAR CoNutrcron, to man who is trying to get on board when car and platform are crowded— " Better wait for the next car, sir, only three minutes behind this one, sir. We are packed full." Man pushes on all the same. Says indignantly— " Street cars are for the accommodation of the public, ain't they ? " Another day: Same man seated in the car. People crowding in and filling the aisle. He growls— 'Strange that people wilt croud in when they see a car is crowded. Ought to be a law to prevent it." SAID an Irishman to a telegraph clerk, "Do you charge for the address in a message?"" No," replied the opyrater. "And do you charge a man for signing his name, sir ?" "No, air." "Wed, then, 1 jist want me brother to know I'm here, an' so will ye plase send this—" To John M`Flinn, at New-York—signed, Patrick M`Flinn ?" A TALKATIVE child annoyed her mother by her remarks on the visitors who came to the house. On one occasion a gentleman was expected whose nose by some unlucky incident was nearly flattened on his face. The mother cautioned the child beforehand to say nothing about this pecu- liarity. Imagine her consternation, then, when the little one exclaimed in the presence of the gentleman, "Ma, you told me not to say anything about Mr. Smith's Hose! why, he hasn't got any nose, mamma !" SHERIDAN was one day much annoyed by a fellow-member of the House of Commons who kept crying out every few minutes, " hear, hear. During the debate, he took occasion to describe a political contemporary that wished to play rogue, but had only sense enough to act fool. Where I" exclaimed he, with great emphasis, "where shall we find a more foolish knave, or a more knavish fool than he?" "Hear, hear !" was shouted by the troublesome member. Sheridan turned round, and, thanking him for the prompt information, sat down amid a general roar of laughter. THE Emperor was reviewing a body of infantry, when his eye was caught by a drummer with only one arm, but who was still playing. "Where is your left arm ?" said he. "At Solferino, sire. You shall have a pension of 400 f. from my private purse." "And if I should leave the other on the road, sire ?" "This," replied Napoleon, pointing to his own rosette of an officer of the Legion of Honour. "The cross 1" exclaimed the soldier; and carried away by a transport of enthusiasm, the new Por- senna, with the remaining arm, drew his sabre, and at one vigorous blow cut it clean off. The ques- tion here is, how he did it?

Minisms, Bishop of Copenhagen, was noted for his absence of mind. He was accustomed, when- ever his duties summoned him from home, to hang a placard on his door announcing, for the benefit of any chance visitor, that he would return at a cer- tain hour. One day, being obliged to attend to some important business in the town, he affixed the usual notice, and, his errand accomplished, came home and ascended the stairs leading to his modest apartment. On arriving opposite his door, he glanced mechanically at the placard, and, entirely unconscious of his own identity, concluded that he was too early, and waited outside until the clock struck, when he suddenly recollected who and where he was, and let himself in.

Mr following unique story is told of Tiger Tail, the Seminole chief. A sewina-machine agent drifted into his dominion one cl:y and set up a machine in Tiger Tail's tent. The old chief with great deliberation watched him put it through its paces. He then rose, brushed the agent to one side, and seating himself, adjusted his feet in the treadle. He started the wheel and found that he could make it go. He sewed up one piece of cloth and down another, and then gravely and critically examined his work. At last he spi),2ared to be satisfied that it was all right. He then turned quietly to his wives, who had watched the proceed- ings with interest, and kicked them, one after the other, out of his tent.

Oh, I'se gwine ter whop .him fur he shain't treat me dater, way an' 'scape." " What's the matter ? " asked a man, stopping at the fence and addressing the woman. " W'y, dat triflin' boy o' mine hab put me trouble, (let's de matter." What did he do?" " W'y, he slipped in dar whar I wax washin' an' eat up all dat soft soap." "You don't tell me that he ate soap?" " Co'se I does, fur.dat's what he done. Never seed sich er as dat in my life. Hit sometime 'peers ter me dat de blame boy acts like he wuz mos' starbed to def, an' dat, too, when he knows Igin him nearly er whole catfish head day befce yistidy. Oh, I'm gwine ter whup him fur eatin' soap like he wns haungry." Y oung writer: "Do you keep all kinds of pans?. -- Mr. Balfour posing as a patron of the Press, is in- describably delicious when we remember that with seven exceptions every editor of a Nationalist newspaper in Ireland—including Mr. T.D.Sullivan, who was at the time Lord Mayor of Dublin—was prosecuteffunder Mr. Balfour's Coercion regime.

Mr. Ritchie, "The Lancet" much regrets to' hear, is again indisposed. Re is unfortunately suffering from a recurrence of the abscess with which he was troubled a year ago. This has been -elieved by operation, but will involve his absence from public duties for a brief period.

It is stated on good authority that his Grace Archbishop Vaughan will not go to Rome for the purpose of receiving the pallium. It will be dis- patched from Rome at the June Consistory. His jurisdiction over the province as Archbishop of Westminster will date from his reception of the pallium.

A member of the House of Commons who is likely to have special information es to the expec- tations in official quarters states positively that the dissolution will be gazetted on Tuesday, June 28. He also expresses the opinion—which seems now to be generally shared on the Conservative benches— that an announcement on the subject will be forth- coming before the Whitsuntide holiday's.

Not the least urgent reason for not postponing the dissolution till next year is the severe strain to which members who are seeking re-election are subject. A well-known member of the .house in- formed me the other day with a merry twinkle that since the present session had commenced all the clubs and associations, and institutions and placts of worship in the constituencies had sud- denly discovered an urgent need of funds. And, said my friend, thay will not cease to want funds till the election is over. '

One of the sons of the late Charles Dickens, who is M.P. for Wilcaunia, New South Wales, appears to have inherited some at least of his distinguished father's humour. Recently he attended a meeting of his eonstituents, and had to speak after a fellow member named Willis,whose oration Was somewhat protracted. "My late father," said Mr. Dickens, ' is reported to have once said Barkis is willin but if he bad been here now be would say • Willis is barkinV "

Mr. Labouchere, in company with Sir Walter Foster, Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Winterbotham, Alfred Thomas, and Mr. Spencer Balfour, has drawn up a scheme of pensions for old age. The main principle is to provide for persons entirely without income, or with income not exceeding 3s. a week, a weekly pension of bs. The scheme would be worked through the County Council, the necessary funds being raised by a county rate, to be divided equally between owner and occupier.

Leading coalownors'in the House of Commons express the opinion that the Durham owners will not yield an inch on the question of a reduction of per cent. in wages. In justification of this attitude it is pointed out that the state of the mar- kets would reasonably warrant a demand for a 15 per cent. reduction, and that would take no account of the damage which has accrued to the collieries during the striking, and which it is contended a 40 per cent. reduction would not cover,

Lord Salisbury is now trying to explain away his seditious speech. His answer to Sir W. Harcourt, given through his secretary, is that "in no part of Lord Salisbury's speech were the words Let Ulster rebel' used, nor, indeed, any words which could properly be so interpreted." Of course, the exact words were not used, but the only, and therefore the proper, interpretation tb at could be placed upon them came to the same thing. Lord Salisbury is a diplomatist, credited generally with caution and an ability to veil his meaning in words. Be is not a Hyde Park orator, and although he may mean the same thing he does not say it in the same language.

"Some hitch has arisen in the matter of the de- igns for the new coinage!' • 1 hope that the hitch- may lead to a more rational treatment of our coin- age. It is now six iieeks. 6inee the recommends- 1 tions of the committee were placed in the hands of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and no one yet knows what decision has been arrived at. Air. Goschen or somebody else made a fine bungle of the previous attempt at reform, and even now it is not contemplated to put the value on the coins. This, one would naturally think, is the first reform which should be carried out. Coins in every other country bear their value stamped on their face. On some of our coins the face value is stated, and that makes it all the more absurd why it should not appear on all.the new coins.

A pathetic description of the condition of the men at Middlesbrough thrown out of employment through the Durham strike is given by the "Daily News ' special correspondent. There are 1,298 skilled workmen, foremen, and overseers breaking slag as if they were convicts in a penal settlement. These men, who a few weeks ago were earning good wages, " have been found guilty of the crime of destitution—or, rather, they have been convicted of the crime of having their work taken away from them for no conceivable fault of their own.' Sub- scriptions are flowing in very slowly to relieve the starving wives and children of these men, who are reduced to a state of pauperism. The present deplorable state of things cannot last long • but meanwhile the charitable should alleviate the suffer- ings of theseunfortunates who are in want by send- ing,subscriptions to:the Lord Mayor at the Mansion House.

The resolution adopted at Hyde Park, on Sunday was reasonable and justifiable. It claimed better terms both as to hours and wages for railway ser- vants, and it wisely enforced its claim by calling upon all railway men to join either the Amalgam- ated Society ot Railway Servants or the General Railway Workers' Union, so that their combination may be efficient and may assist them to enforce their just demands. The public have continued to be shocked—we do not think we can use a milder phrase—with the disclosures as to the length of hours worked by many railway servants which have been made in the evidence brought before the committee of the House of Commons. That com- mittee is by no means a body prejudiced in favour of the men, and yet it can scarcely be doubted that it will be obliged to make some strong recommend- ations in the very direction of the resolution passed in Hyde Park. It is high time that we had the re- port of this committee; and if the meeting does nothing else than expedite the deliberations of that body it will not be without good effect.' .

Two American ladies were presented in the dip- I lornatic circle at Monday's Drawing Room. They were Mrs. Post, the wife of Major Post, the newly married military attache tb, the American Legation, and Miss Anderson, the sister of Mr. Larr Anderson, Mr. Lincoln's second secretary. In the general circle, ten or a dozen more of our dainty cousins from over the Atlantic made their salaams to Prin- cess Christian.

It was amusing to notice the absolute noncbal, ance with which the spectators criticised the appearanoe of those who were making their way to the Drawing Room. The splendid coach of the Turkish Embassy containing Rustem Pasha, Morel Bey, and Madame Morel excited a good deal of attention, and the glittering uniform and red fezzes created great delight. "Don't be look wicked ?" a remark made by a girl in the crowd, had the effect of bringing a smile to Rustem's diplomatie coun- tenance. The Portuguese Minister, who followed shortly, and whose fierce black moustache and imperial and saturnine NiEage were well, set off by the blue uniform glittering with gold, received a perfect ovation. The women in the crowd criticised him in a strain of broad compliment, which ought to have made him blush. "My ! this is splendid!" screamed a vivacious young thing, but Don 'Aix moved not a hair. The members of the Siamese legation, who looked like a party of good little boys in fancy dress, evoked screams of delight, but the Chinese Minister, in his national dressing gown, I cap, and pigtail, was csrtainly the success of the diplomatic procession.

And noar at last Jack. acted as he ought to have done long before, that is, he raised his head and looked his questioner full in the face. "And if I do?" he asked piteously, and yet with proud sorrow, "It is my only crime, and the punishment has come with it God knows I have struggled against the feeling, and tried to believe that it 'was only friendship, it was as great a shock to me as to you, when I found it out, Oallerley, and I don't now know even how it happened. I have seen little of women, and she has been so kind to me 1"

The young fellow spoke so simply, and with such honest sorrow, that he must needs have awakened some pity in Sir Lancelot's heart, had it not been eompletely hardened by unworthy suspicion. But the winsome manner only went against poor Jack, by provoking jealous comparisons in hie favour. Sir Lancelot Callerley could not forget._ that young Breamish had twenty years to the good as a lov.er. . Besides, the Callerley temper was surging and rioting through the baronet's veins, and thus honest confession'did not tend to quiet it. Instead, hp let it loose in a flood of violent, unjust, scathing language; cursed Jack deeply, and cursed still more his OWII folly in believing in any goodness or 'virtue whatever ; cursed Silvia, because she could smile in his face, while she was, in all probability, deceiving him. ' It was here that Jack first comprehended the possibility that she—his angel of purity and gool treirs=76.s jeukted by her husband. The blOOd mounted to his face, lie stamped his foot with sudden affger. "Are you mad ?" he said, in hot anger, "Yes, you must be mad to forget yourself so far as to Speak of your wife in that fashion. Great Heavens ! I never dreamt that you could doubt her. Poi myself, blame me as you choose, and I admit that I am to blame," hanging his head for a moment, "though I swear to you that my thoughts of her have never been impure; and, indeed, save weak- ness, I have little to be ashamed of ; but for her— why, she is as innocent of wrong as any child. Do you hear me, Callerley; do you hear me, madman that you are ?" " Wrong ? Perhaps, in your sense of the word— who knows? Do I care to have possession of a body, if the soul is in another's keeping? Do I care for the semblance of fidelity, if you have stolen her heart—" "You are wrong—utterly and absolutely wrong! If any other man had said as much I should have killed him on the spot for the insult that it implies to her. How can I convince you? Oh, how can I make him see you as you are—my poor Silvia?" The words were scarcely out of his mouth before Sir Lancelot struck him furiously across the face with a riding whip, and then threw it away. , "No man shall live• to speak of Lady Callerley as his poor Silvia, if I can hinder him ! It is me you must kill before you have the right to do that, me—poor Silvia's husband. One of us two must die. You recognise that necessity, I hope ?" 'Jack bowed his head sadly. God knows he had no wish to kill Sir Lancelot; but there are insults no gentleman ought to bear tamely. The mark of the angry man's blow was red on his cheek, and it stung and smarted no little ; but for that he cared nothing. Ile knew that,this man, who soughehis life under a misapprehension, was the one Silvia really loved' ; and felt himself the sport of a cruel ta4,te that he could not explain this at once to Sir neelot. "Would that WA could fight now, at once, and haVe it over)" spoke on the baronet hurredly, "why in the noniti of all folly has the good old fashion of wearing swords become obsolete. But after all we May still solve that difficulty. Teddy, you carry a pistol, and so do I. What need then for further delay? • The moon has risen above the clouds, and if we stand where it shines .yonder—?" "You must allow me, Callerley," interposed Teddy Wynne, at this juncture, "though you do choose to treat me with contempt, you must at least admit that I have.had some little experience in affairs of honour. Well then, I tell you this candidly, and 'pon my word it is a serious matter. If you fight now, and without either seconds or a doctor, it will be murder. nothinv more nor less." "Murder ?" repeated his brother-in-law mechani- cally; but the words did not seem to convey any impression to him. Perhaps it really was murder that lay hidden in his heart; b.nd so it came to pass that the name was familiar. Teddy's plumes were evidently ruffled, for he put on 'his grandest air, and chose his language with Joint- sonian care. "Yes, that is what it will be, and I for one am not inclined to be mixed up with anything so de- grading, or so vulgar! You must appoint a friend, Callerley, and we—he and I that is—will arrange the time and place for a meeting. Mr. Brearnish, after the manner in which that man has dared to speak of my sister:--his wife—my sympathies have entirely gone over to your side; and I shall be proud to act as your second, that is if you care to accept me in that capacity. And by Gad, sir, after you have done with him, I must also have a reckoning, for the sake of the honour of my family."

At sunset on Callerley sands. Such was the settled time and pl. Tile- choice of weapons was given to Jack, and he deCided upon pistols. Though a fair shot..•iyith a gun, he knew little about the smaller weapons ; but calculated that if they were used the affair :would be sooner over. Besides, he knew himself accomplished in the use of the rapier, and was quixotically determined that Sir Lancelot should have every advantage. It would only make the latter more angry if he discovered—as he was pretty 'certain to do after a few passes—that his adver- sary was simply parrying, not dealing thrusts. Lady Callerley was sitting by the window of her room' looking out upon the Dutch garden, when Sir Lancelot prepared to keep his appointment on Callerley sands. The door was ajar, and as he passed it he saw the dainty figure within and paused irresolute. Perhaps it was the last look he might ever have of her; and though he hated her for having, as he thought, deceived and wronged him; nevertheless, her beauty had power over his senses. He entered, and crossing the room, stood by her side. Silvia's thoughts were of him, and he seemed to come as in answer to these same thoughts. Since the talk with Jack Breamish in which he had pleaded Sir Lancelot's strange temper and family peculiarities as excuse for any apparent marital-coldness, Lady Callerley had begun to doubt whAesctle fult,of eptFangement did AU, after all, lie principally with heiself: , Oh, that she could muster courage, and taking her fate in her own hands, make some effort to sur- mount this indefinable barrier which lay between her heart and the heart wherein she longed to dwell as lover, queen and wife I Often did she steal glances at the dark, stern face of her husband, hoping for some sign of tender reTenting ; but ever at such periods did her soul sink within lier. If he should put her coldly aside as childish and fanciful, and repel her timidly proferred love—why then her heart would break indeed for very shame and sorrow. ' - When he now drew near to her She began to tremble. It was many a long day since he had sought her apartments. Had he come to make his peace, come to tell her that he forgave her silly petulance, and was prepared to allow her to try to under- stand, an to be one with him in soul? God grant it I Her small hands were clasped upon each other nervously, and she looked up at him in piteous mute appeal. "How do you manage to get that expression into your eyes ?" he asked, in a low, hoarse voice, "One would say you loved and were afraid of me if—if one did not know differently." Silvia forgot to resentthe last words, in her eager- ness to answer the others. She now clasped her hands and laid them upon his arm. "And so I do, and so I am," she said quickly. "Oh, Lancelot, why do • you not give me another chance? I was so young, and I did not under- stand." "Silence, girl lam not to be deceived any longer. You have an angel's face, but God alone knows your heart." Lady Callerley drew back alarmed. The fire of anger burning in his deep set eyes was terrible to witness. Could it be that the doom of the Caller- leys had descended upon him in the form of in- sanity? Surely no man in his senses could wear such a look? , But her courage revived, almost immediately. If he meant to kill her, as his looks seemed to imply, at least he should not insult her first with- out some protest against it. By a great effort she , forced herself to stand upright, holding by the wall Cn.• to steady her; and then she looked him in the face, with the proud dignity of a true wife. div.head: STAGE W-I-TTA-N-D-TWAGGERY. aozQ
div.p: STAGE W-I-TTA-N-D-TWAGGERY. aozQ

A popular actor and dratiatist, Mr. Kenny,- never let an opportunity slip of making a joke or perpet- rating a pun. While drinking a glass of wine ime day he inadvertently swallowed'a small substance, which nearly choked him. A friend, seeing his distress, and being anxious to Proclaim to the com- pany the sad state of 'the case, 'exclaimed, "It is cork gone down the wrong way." "I d—d—don't know whether it is the wrong way to Cork," grasped the barely-recovered punster; "but it seems a very likely way to Killienny." What an incorrigible joker Sothern was everyone knows, and quite as bad was To Flynn,the famous American comedian. Perhaps the funniest story related of him has reference to the time when he' was playing at the Bowery Theatre, New York.: During his engagement the celebrated Junius Booth came to "star" there,upon which nccasion "Julius Omar" was produced, Booth being Cassius, .1-larab- lin (the manager) Brutus, and/ John Woodhull, Mark Antony. Hamblin, after dressing, repaired to the greenroom, and having a bad cold,which some- what impaired his speech, asked Flynn what he' could do for it. Toni, who never lost the chance of a joke, let it hit where it would, said, "Use my ' remedy." "What's that ?" asked'llamblin. "Why get some vinegar in a teacup, put some snuff in it, mix the two together, pour it into your band, and inhale it throggh your nose." Hamblin, not thinking of the consequences, im- mediately took a sufficient quantity of this won- derful remedy to produce a fit of sneezing, which he found very difficult to overcome. After going upon the stage, he saluted the audience with a sneeze, and struggled hard to smother the effects of the snuff, but without avail. He began—" What is it that you would (sneeze) impart to me? If it be aught toward the general good .(hang the snuff), set honour in one eye (sneeze) and death in the other,and I will look(sneeze) on both indifferently, For let the gods so speed Me; I love (sneeze) the name of (sneeze) honour more than I fear death. (curse that Flynn!)" All his efforts to check the effects of Flynn's remedy,which proved worse than the disease, were unavailing. The sneezing became contagious with the Bowery boys, for directly after one of Brutus's convulsions an immense sneeze would echo from the audience. Flynn Eat in the boxes enjoying Hamblin's discomfort. What rendered the affaiernore ludicrous was that Hamblin several times attempted to sneeze,but fill- ing,, the audience did it for him I and then when they expected the tietor would remain quiet, he would give another sneeze, which would cause the whole house to roar with laughter, thus converting the tragedy into a laughable farce. After the play Hamblin rushed• into.the green- room and said to Flynn, "What in the name: of Heaven did you advise me to take that infernal mess for I"' Tom, standing before the grate with his hands under his coat-tails, replied with tbe utmost cool- ness, "Why, it always cures me of .a 'cold in the head, Mr. Ifamblin, when I take it," and as the sneezing Beaus left the room Flynn turned to Booth, who had been standing in one corner enjoy- ing the joke, and said, "Why, Junius, my boy, I never thought before that your performance of Cassius was to be sneezed at 1" Of a famous French actor's dry hintour many instances are recorded. Meeting one day a pretty actress whose lover had jilted her, he opened the door of her coup, and did all that was in his power to console her. But she would not be comforted. "No, no," she cried, "I can never smile again! I must drown myself?" "Very well," said her hearer, calmly shutting the d00r,," we shall meet at the Morgue. Coachman, ,drive this lady to the river." Yet he once meditated suicide himself, and, having loaded a pistol, called it a friend and brother actor to receive his /lying wishes. The friend did not attempt to dissuade him, but calmly jotted down the desired requests. Then, while his com- panion was writing a farewell letter, he took lip the pistol and began examining it. It was cocked, and the muzzle was pointing straight at the intend- ing suicide, when that individual suddenly ducked with remarkable agility under the table, crying, "Look out! The infernal thing is loaded." Foote, the dramatist, was once the author of an extremely practical pun. Having in one of his

- that gentleman waited on the mimic, and indig- natly complained of the injury his character had sustained through his being taken off upon the stage. The comedian having vainly endeavoured to laugh his visitor into good humour, at length observed," well as you seem displeased at my tak- ing you off, you shall immediately see me take myself off !" The enraged actor was pacified, and Foote, taking up his hat, walked out of the room. O'Brien waited an hour before he saw the joke, and found that he would have to wait longer still be- fore he saw the joker. So he, too, "took himself off." An ercinent, but at times rather absent-minded, special pleader, being at a theatre witnessing the play of • Macbeth," allowed his thoughts to wan- der away from the performance to an elaborate case he had on hand. Coming to the scene where Macbeth questions the witches in the cavern, "What is that ye do?" and they answer, "IA deed without a name," his ear just caught the phrase. and suddenly turning to a friend, he said audibly, " What's that? A deed without a name. Pooh ! nonesense I a deed without a name is void, of course."

div.head: CHARGE OF CUTTING AND WOUNDING
div.p: CHARGE OF CUTTING AND WOUNDING
A WIFE.

At the Warrington borough police court on Mon- day morning, before the Mayor and Alderman Harrison, James Kelly, was charged with cutting and wounding his wife Mary Kelly on Sunday ,norn- ' ing last. The complainant who appeared with her head bandaged, said she lodged with Mrs. Narroway at 9, Watkin-street. On Saturday evening as her husband did not come home she went in search of him, found him drinking, and brought him home, about o'clock. As they were going home she asked him for some money to get something to eat, and he said he had none. After she got him in he went out again, and returned about ten o'clock. The door was then locked, but he got in through a broken window. He went to bed immediately, but as he had threatened her before he went to bed she slept on‘the sofa all night. He got up about four o'clock the next morning, and began beating her about the head with his fists. She screamed out, and Mrs. Narroway came down and took her away from him. She stepped across the kitchen to , get out of his way, and he followed her and said he would kill her, and struck her in the side of the head with a knife, and swore he would swing for her. She bled from the head, and she went outside the house and remained there, till a constable came. She after- wards had her wound dressed at the Infirmary.—Dr. Henry Langdale, junior house surgeon there, deposed that the wound was an inch and a quarter long and less than a quarter of an inch deep. He apprehended no danger from it, as it was not serious.—Eliza Narrc way, the landlady at the prisoner's lodgings, gave corroborative evidence. She was woke by Mrs. Kelly screaming, and found the pris- oner beating her as she lay on the sofa. She separated ' I them, and he pulled a knife out of the table drawer and stabbed his wife with it, then threw the knife into the fireplace. She sent for the police and handed , the knife to the constable.—John Henderson, a lodger I at Mrs. Narroway's, said be went dovrnstaiis on hearing the screams, and found blood on the hearth, the knife in the fireplace, and Mrs. Kelly bleeding. He told the prisoner he ought to be ashamed of himself for stabbing his wife, and he struck witness more than once. He struck his fist on the table and swore, and said he would punck her ribs and kill her, if he should swing for it. When Mrs. Kelly went outside he ran at her again, and 'witness ran out after him and would not let him do anything. He said he would kill her and him too. He was quite sober. He asked witness to gn out to the back to fight but he had no boots on, and while he was putting them on Kelly pulled out his pocket knife and opened It with the intention of stabbing him with it by way of the first blow.—The prisoner said Henderson struck him before this.—P.C. Brewen deposed to being sent for, and on his way see- ing the prisoner near his own home, who, on sight of him ran away, and winless caught him in Winwick-st. He there dropped a pocket knife, which he had open in his hand. He said he did not care whether he ha killed his wife or not, and on being charged at the Station, made no reply.—The prisoner, on being charged in the usual way, said he had nothing- to say, but that he was very sorry for what had happened ,though he had been aggravated by his wife taking his money from ' lim.—He was committed to the Assizes.

div.head: CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
div.p: THE CURSE OF THE CALLERLEYS.
BY LILLIAS WASSERMAN, Author of "Some Fisher Folk," "Judith," "Where the North Wind Blows," ,the.; the.
CITAPTER XLIL THE CA#T-LENGL

The road along which Jack set out was the same that Dick Daglish had been riding along upon that night when he fled into the wood for refuge from his pursuers, and came suddenly upon the ghastly spectacle of the body of limes, the coast-guard, hanging upon a tree there. Since the discovery of the murder the country folk had pronounced this road to be haunted, and with one accord shunned the vicinity of the wood after nightfall. There were those ready jto swear that they had seen the face of the murdered man peering out at thern from amongst the trees; while others had had their steps quickened by the sound of dismal groans proceeding from the depths of the plantation. Jack Breamish laughed at these super- stitious fancies when he was sober, and of course a tipsy man fears nothing while he is pot-valiant; but as the effect of the wine did out of him under the sobering influence of the cold and the darkness, he began to wish that he had pocketed his pride, and slept at his brother's house ; instead of deciding to plod along ILiatalazk and dreary moorland road to Farmer Toddi farm. , 7.•-7 . • To be lure Madam'•ls gibes Wive not easy to bear wall, and now more tan ever did she know how to barb her darts, since she guessed Jack's poor secrlit, and used to allude to it in a furtive manner, to his utter discomfiture. It is difficult to wage war with women. Their sex protects them from , anything in the shape of retaliation, unless a man descends to brutality. And Madam was so skilled in the art of veiling her sarcasms, that it was almost impossible to resent them openly. Besides, her temper would be none of the best after the hubbub had subsided. Although in some matters, such as the entertaining of his frieilds and neighbours, and the keeping up the reputation for open and generous hospitality for which his family was famous, the Squire managed to hold his own and get his way, it was not without a struggle; nor was the domestic atmosphere of Brownish Hall pleasant to breathe , for some days after the master of the house had asserted himself. Nevertheless, Jack thought longingly of the good fires and the comfort he was leaving ; as he set his face to the wind, and heard it whistle eerily through the leafless branches of the trees o'er- head. A fitful moonlight struggled with a cloudy sky; and the lights that went and came—glinting and flickering here and there upon the silver stein of a birch, or upon the water of a mountain burn, had a most weird and uncanny effect. Jack could not help reflecting that this was exactly the sort of night for ghosts to be abroad in, and though he did not believe in them, he did not altogether like the notion. After all he was North-country bred, and it is difficult to entirely eradicate superstition, when hereditary tendencies saffi training are all in its No vengeance—save, perhaps, the vengeance taken by Heaven upon the crew of the Bonny Bess —had as yet fallen upon the murderers; and it was pretty certain that those cons,orned were not all in- cluded in the drowned smugglers. 'What more likely than that the spirit of the murdered should wander restlessly upon earth until blood had been shed for blood, and life for life ? Just as this pleasant idea occurred to Jack, he caught sight of a figure sitting upon the low parapet of a wall immediately in front of him, and he stopped short in alarm. The figure leapt from the low parapet wlitte it was sitting, and advanced rather unsteadily into the middle of the path, just at the point where a patch of moonlightlfell athivart it, confronting Jack with a vision of a dapper little man in knee breeches and cocked hat, in place of the ghost of the revenue officer which ought properly to have appeared there. "A word with you, Mr. Jack Breamish !" said this figure, suddenly, "I've been waiting of you ' this—{hiccup)—hour or so, sir, to tell you, sir, that 'Br. seta -7, you re a—a blackguard—a low fellow—and— (hiccup)—devilishly cold and—and uncomfortable it's been, sir, let me assure you that, on the honour of a—(hiccup)—gentleman ! "Why, Teddy? Mr. Wynne, what on earth is the matter ?" cried Jack, surprised, and experienc- ing as complete a shock as though he had just taken a header into cold water. The shock had one good effect, however, for it helped to restore him to his senses. " Matter ? Matter enough surely when a— (hiecuph—a lady's name is used in such a—a way as to suggest comparison—comparison, sirr with your Phillises and your—(hiccup)—your Chloes—your light o' loves? By God, sir, you must answer to me for your damned impertinence in bringing my sister's name into such company—you naust—" Did you did you hear me give that 'j toast ? " asked Jack simply, "I thought you were I asleep !" "No, sir, I was not asleep, or drunk either, as— j (hiticup)—l suppose you are pleased to insinuate! j I heard you refer to my—(hiccup)—my sister, Lady ' Callerley, as though her name, Silvia, were common property, like those of your—your ordinary country wenches. What right have you to speak of Lady*Callerley, as Silvia, eh, sir, answer me that jj,i,

- "Pardon me for interrupting you, Teddy, but this is Iny business r broke in a stern voice at this moment." Was Jack dreaming, he wondered; rubbing his eyes, and staring vacantly at the new copier, who appeared to start out of the shadow of the trees which overhung the bridge. No, that voice, and those dark eyes when a sombre fire of hatred burned, were too real to belong to a dream !

Sir Lancelot put aside Teddy as though he were a child, and faced Jack himself. "It is to me you must answer for the liberty you have taken, Jack Breamish ! What have you got to .say on the subject—what excuse—what devilish lie—or more devilish truth, perhaps—can you bring forward to serve as excuse for the liberty ?" " Good Heavens, Callerley I You do not suppose I' meant the least disrespect to Silvia, to Lady Callerley ? I would have cut out my tongue rather than that! What can I say? She is as far abcrie me as the angels, and as pure; how is it possible that I should fail to know it, and to reverence her accordingly ?" "Is it angels you think of over your cups ?" asked Teddy, with scorn. But Callerley waved him off again. "Be quiet, boy! You must not interfere in this, I tell you. Mr. Breamish, lam waiting to hear you out!" There was no desire for justice at the bottom of the careful quietude of. Sir Lancelot's mode of address. Indeed, there was something instead, which instinctively made Jack shudder, though he was no coward. A vengeful, terrible passion was there suppressed and held down by a powerful will, a will that only bided its time to strike. And those gloomy eyes were fixed on Jack, as though there was one qua. tion which must be answered; and which he, and he alone, could answer. The seeds of suspicion so industriously and insidiously sown for months, had taken. root, and were twining themselves round Sir Lancelot's very heartstrings; choking, by their pestilent grasp, all the more generous growths. Poor Jack! He was quite sober enough now to recognise the mischief he had wrotight ; but for ! the life of him he could not see the way to mend ' matters. • "What can I say ?" he stammered, his eyes fall- ing before those which would fain have read the secret of his soul, and reached the intiost recesses for what it expected to find there, "-I was—Caller- ley, you know I was overcome, or I would never have brought out her name. I declare that' it is absolutely sacred to me !" " Sacred ? And you make it a jest for drunken fools ?" commented Callerley, with bitterness, "Is anything held sacred nowadays? Out of the fulness of the heart the mouth speaketh. Had you not dared to think of her as you ought not and had no right to do, you never had breathed her name at such a time; and if you say otherwise, I will give you the lie." Jack sighed, and kept his eyes fixed on the ground. I could not help it—Callerley !" he stammered weakly, "I was overcome, you must • have seen it! There is nothing else in it indeed, , you must believe tne I" The intense gaze of the dark eyes fixed upon him • drew his upward irresistibly, and Jack knew that concealment was no longer possible. "You lie 1" said Sir Lancelot, with slow distinct- ness. • "No, no ! you must believe 1" gasped the other. "You lie I can see the lie written all over you in letters of fire. You love my wife 1"

for his love of the excitemeht of a row. He trailed his coat with persistence ; but, to his great vexation, warned by past experience, no one would tread on the tail of it. The fact was that people knew him so well that they kept out of his way, and if sufficiently unfor- tunate to be brought into contact, or worse still, opposition to him, they gave way at once; recog- nising that any contradiction would afford him the longed-for pretext for a quarrel. The conciliatory policy was not, however, so much because they were afraid, as because they knew that he really had ho animus against them personally—being very good-hearted at bottom— but simply wanted a row as other people wanted drink, or play, or fox-hunting, for the mere love and exiternent of it. And it was not pleasant to folks to be treated as ninepins. • Tom Scott therefore accepted the office proffered him, delightedly; and hoped that before the duel was over he should be able to rise to a principal, instead of a subordinate part. Teddy Wynne, for example, would be none the worse of a good licking to take the nonsense out of him, since the way he looked at people through that eyeglass of his was most offensive to anyone acutely conscious of coun- trified appearance and attire. All the same it would not be a very gallant victory to conquer such a hop o' my thumb; and Tom Scott found imper- tinence easier to forgive in so small a man, than lie watill have done in a foeman more worthy of his
i

nisn's -iiiiiten—ae a continuous struggle xfro—a the devil walk abroad clothed in velvet, and wear- ing a feather in his cap? Are there no hot blooded fools) nowadays into whose ears he can whisper soft ani•insidious lies, instilling the elements of deceit and treachery, awakening within thenithe foulest passiOns ; until lust and jealousy and impurity sully and degrade the finest natures ; and there are no houses left where men can see the re- flection of divinity in woman and where children may learn to know of heaven through their mother's lips and eyes !" "You are unjust to the world, Lancelot There are such homes and such mothers and—and wives still; I am certain." "I do not believe It! I will not believe it—for then I should have to blame fate in that it had singled me out for wrongs whichfare easier to bear when one imagines them common to humanity." "Why do you talk so wiklly—dear—husband ?" asked Silvia, with timid hesitation then, going cilbser to him, she gazed up into his race with the same piteous, pleading expression at which he had expressed surprise, when first he entered the

room. "What can I say to move you ?" she went on after a pause, with gentle and persistent patience* "if that lam sorry for the past, you will not b4ve me. If I say that II love yen now—, "Too late for that," broke in Sir Lancelot, in harsh voice," Once I might have accepted that se truth—but not now—not now! Say nothinjl4' That is best, much best. Your eyes speak. you only too eloquently, but I must not ne• no, I must not believe them! They are false 1401 set to lure a man to hell. Nevertheless, becau.se your beauty and your winsomeness, and not because of any faith I have left in you, I shall hold you in 7F my arms, and kiss you once again." "Not so. Give me your respect at least, if yo* cannot give me your love !" pleaded the wife, draw-, - big back from him. In vain. With a laugh that grated on her nerves as the' ; demonical laughter of a demon might have, done, Sir Lancelot caught and held her in a and passionate embrace, and kissed her lips a dozen times over. 5. "Sweetest of lips, I have had the last of pot!, he cried, a wicked triumph lighting 1113 his gri; visage. "Cone what come may, my kisses are t latest Good-bye Lady Callerley, and do 114 forget my words. 'Be good, if possible; and if YD* cannot be good, at least be merciful !" "Whither do you go, and why is it to be gnoc!" bye?" asked Silvia, alarmed at something in ha manner. But no answer came to her enquiry, and uPOII ' looking round she saw that she was alone. div.head: GENEII,AL ELECTIbIst
div.p: THE GENEII,AL ELECTIbIst
TCRIES EXPECT A LIBERAL MAJORth:

A special correspondent writes :—I have good reason to believe that the dissolution will take place on, or about the 28th of June. In that event the great majoriti. of the borough elections would be over by the Bth on 9th of July, and, with the exception of some of the more remote counties, the whole elections would be complete by the 18th or 20th of that month. Ministers estimate that Mr. Gladstone will have a majority of between twenty and thirty, and should this expectation be justi- fied, they will not resign, but will meet Parliament. They anticipate that twenty or twenty-five ihembers of the Redmond party in the next Parliament will not join in a vote of no confidence in the Government until Mr. Gladstone produces his Home Rule scheme.
THE ROBBERY FROM CAPTAIN VERNEY AN EARLESTOWN MAN IN TROUBLE.

William Whiteman a rough-looking individual, who said he came from Earlestown, was brought before Alderman Thomas, at the Crewe Borough Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing a bag, containing £2O in money, and other articles, at Crewe Station' on Thursday night. Detective-Inspector Freeboroughex- plained that the bag which the prisoner was charged with stealing belonged to Captain Verney, who passed through Crewe on Thursday night. The prisoner said: "I have not stolen the money, or anything else you found in my possession. About six p.m. on Thursday I came straight from Chester to Crewe station. I went straight off the station to my lodgings, and did not come on again that night. The money and purse pound on me I found on the highway, between Warrington and Chester." Detective-Inspector Freeborough said on the evidence he wished to ask for a remand, and the prisoner was accordingly remanded till Tuesday. ' On Tuesday Whiteman was further remanded till Tuesday next.

div.head: YLOODS IN AMERICA.
div.p: THE YLOODS IN AMERICA.
ENORMOUS LOSSES OF PROPERTY.
°SIXTY PFRSONS DROWNED,

The river Mississippi was on Monday said to be only a few inches below the terrible flood of 1883. Tha traffic across the river bridges and along the level rail- ways is suspended, and for miles along the river farms are deserted and crops ruined, while numerous cases of drowning are reported. NEW YORK, TRIIRSDAT.—It is estimated that some 8,000 persons have been driven from their homes in Sioux City and the vicinity in consequence of the floods and eleven persons are known to have been drowned. All business has been suspended. The stockyards are inundatedpand the loss of live stock is set down at 2?000 head. Later advice from Sioul eltsi "Stattl that the viratd is slowly subsiding, but that the damage to property amounts to at least 1,500,000 dots. The kiss in the Sioux City and along the Northern Railroad 1 timated at fully gstod,ooct dais. The cititens ate most actively, engaged in plbrilding shelter for the holieless, but the scenes on the ifiVet banks are described as piteous, and it is feared that Ma loss of life will prove to have been appalling. At Spring, dale a woman with a babe in her arms stood for hours at a second-storey window appealing for help, and she was still there at eight o'clock last night. Two men had been drowned in an attempt to rescue her. . . .

SIOUX CITT, THllRSDAY.—Aceording to the latest tele- grams the &ads in this part of the country have caused much lbss of life. The estimates vary, but there seems reason to fear that from sixty to a hundred persons have perithed.

In reference to a statement made on Thursday night in a London evening piper, professedly on 'good author- ity, that £3,000,000 additional capital will be required to complete the Manchesteit Ship Canal, it is authorita, tively stated that there is' no foundation whatever for the assertion. Within a foW days contracts will be let for two sections, and a stafefrisnt will be made immedi- ately afterwards as to the precise amount which will be required. PROPOSED CONVEYANCE or C"ATTLE UP THE

CANAL:'- --- - On Thursday a deputation from:Manchester saw Mr. Chaplain, tho president of the Board of Agriculture, to present to him a request for the creation of Manchester as a landing depot for foreign cattle. The Mayor of Manchester (Mr. Leech), Mr. Aldermali Mark, Alderman Sir John Harwood, Mr. Alderman Thompson; Mr. Alder- man Roberts, Mr. Alderman Read, Councillor Needham town clerk, the medical officer of health, and Mr. Mar- shall Stevens (manager of the Ship Can 'Company) were present. The deputation explained that it was desired to land live cattle on the banks of the canal near Manchester, that they had arranged a site with the Ship Canal Company, that the shipowners engaged in the trade were willing to carry cattle up the canal, and that tliere•was within a fifty miles radius of Manchester a population considerably larger than that in a like area of which London was the ' centre. Mr. Chaplain laid, stress on the danger which might arise in the chance of contagion fram deceased cattle passing up the canal tao the herds grazing on the banks, but this was met by, the reply that at Glasgow, twenty miles up the Clyde; there was a: depot, and thst the navigation of the glyde was in some.cases narrower than the Ship Canal would be. Ultimai4ely the President promised to carefully consider the matter and to let the deputation know his decision.

Siinmon and the Rev. John Taylor, THE CHAIRMAN'S ADDRESS. The Chairman, in his opening address, said the princi- pal purpose of the meeting was to review the wort done during the Connexional year which was drawing to a close. He was glad to say that their successes and their gains were much ia excess of their. losses and failures. (Applause.) There had been an increase of 40 in the inember§hip of the dietriet after malting up the extraordinary loss of 304 members, by deatbS, re- movals, and withdrawals. They would therefore see that even to maintain their own they had always to be labouring and working in the vineyard of the Lord. Then,in addition, they had to rejoice over an increase in the number of their scholars. Conaiderably over 500 scholars had been added to the number of scholars in the district under the care of 30 additional teachers. (Hear, hear.) He the Chairman) rejoiced in these in- creases, because they iadicated that the ,Church, itself was getting into a higher and a diviner life,closely asso- ciated with Ged. The only sure cure for indifference to divine things, and to the services of the sanctuary, was earnest, enthusiastic, Christian work. Enthusiasm was contagious—nothing succeeded like success—and if they could only get their people to be influenced by a spirit of enthusiasm, they 'would be encouraged to prosecute their work with greater diligence. He hoped that next year would be one of great prosperity, and that the pro- ceedings of that meeting would be so influential that its pirit vvould be so genuinely brotherly and kindly, that ,tkily would go to their circuits with their hearts filled with a flame of divine love, and more anxious than they had ever been to win souls for Christ. div.head: WESLEY MEMORIAL.
div.p: THE WESLEY MEMORIAL.

The Rev. J. B. Stoneman reported in regard to the Wesley Centenary Memorial Fund that up to the present £4OO had heen raised in Liverpool district, and he hoped to bring the amount up to £l3OO. This closed the first day's proceedings.

PUBLIC MEETING. In the evening a public meeting was held in the chapel under the presidency of the ''district chairman, Mr. R. Lloyd, and there was a good attendance. The choir led the congregational singing and also rendered several anthems in admirable style. The Chairman in his opening speech urged them to work unremittingly as followers of the prophets and apostles. The Rev. W. R, gunman in the course of an earnest address dealt with the alleged decadence of Methodism.—The Rev. E. Hall, who had a cordial reception, delivered an ad- dress on woman's work in the spread of Christianity, which he dealt with in a highly interesting manner, point- ing out the many spheres of usefulness in which women could engage.—The Rev. John Taylor dealt with the question of foreign missions in an earnest speech.—The customary votes of thanks were passed.

• THE SECOND DAY. The session was resumed on Wednesday morning under the presidency of Mr. Lloyd.—The Rev. E. Hall proposed the following motion : " Resolved that inas- much as the drink traffic is the cause of the greater part of the irreligion, immorality, pauperism, and crime in our midst, and that all Christian effort is baffled and re- tarded by the public-house and beerhouse, and that whilst recognising the efforts of some magistrates anf, County Councillors this meeting declares that no mere transfer of the licensing authority to County Councils ; district Councils, or specially eleeted boards will meet the necessities of the case and. will be satisfied with nothing less than a measure giving to the house- holders in every locality the (Prect veto over the issue tad re-JIM fit 1,411 ticept393 in their area. And celllifki the importanc of the ts- on fregi a religious and e moral standpoint this meeting further urge; V! Christian voters to seriously consider their responsibility to God and man, before they vote for or in any way support those candidates who would not promise to vote in Parliament for so just and righteous a measure."—Mr. T. Gibson seconded and Mr. T. Snape, C.C. supported the motion which Was adopted. The Rev. J. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was Held at the Workhouse cm Wednesday morning. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Davies, Dobson, A. Jolley, Pilling, Shaw, Gill, Longton, Hill, Muir, A. J. Jolley, Fairclough, Swinton, Humphreys, Dig- num, W. Houghton, Smith, Warburton Owen, fib- bert, Mather ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and 'S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) AN OUTBREAK OF MEL

_ The Workhouse Master reported that a fire broke out in the female nurses' sitting-room about nine o'clock at night. It was extinguished as quickly as possible, but no,t before the floor had been partly burned, as well as the carpet and rug. The total damage was estimated at £4 10a., and a claim for this amount had been sent in to the insurance agent. The Workhouse Master ex- plained that the fire had been caused by a hot coal rolling from the grate on to the floor. Fortunately some one entered the room before the fire had gained much of a hold, or otherwise the results might have been serious.

A fishing lugger has been lost off Castietownshend, having been cut in two by an Atlantic liner. A portion of the smack and the hats of her crew have been washed ashore at,Toehead. The lugger was struck during a dense fog, and it is feared that all the crew have perished.

MINING ROYALTIES.

(From "Land and Labour?) An important part of the General Land National- isation Question is that affecting Mining Royalties. These not only differ in pifferent districts, but they Very in "mines situated in the same locality. These irregularities may have arisen from the leases hav- ing been granted when trade was prosperous or the reverse ; or from the mining difficulties being greater in one case than in another; or from differ- ences in the quality of the mineral; and lastly from the geographical position of the field containing it. In the United Kingdom the property of the min- erals is, unless other arrangements have been entered into, vested in the owners of the soil ; in any , case the'nerson working them has to pay for the , right of so doing. To prevent the mine owner leaving large areas of ground and leaving it unworked, fixed rents are charged whether the mineral is worked or not, such fixed rents being regarded as payments on account for future workings. The amount involved in these fixed rents is sometimes very inconvenient to.the lessee. The ironmaster may have to contend with adverse times, when, the state of trade would suggest either a reduction of make or its entire discontinuance. He has, however, not only to face this fixed payment, but he has to keep the mines free from water, and the machinery &c., in good repair. There are cases where .0,0,000 or £30,000 a year would barely suffice to meet the expenditure under these two heads.

The royalty dues paid in Cleveland for ironstone are about 6d. a ton. In Lincolnshire and Nort- hamptonshire they are sometimes double this sum because instead of expensive shafts and machinery being required, the mineral lies near the surface, with a covering of greater or less thickness of sand or rock. In such cases it is not got by simple quarrying. Coal varies in different places, but 6d. to is. per ton may be regarded as common rates. A common rent for limestone is id. to 3d. per ton. In addition to these 'charges the lessee has to pay double rent for all surface damage, and to restore the soil at the end ot his lease or pay its value. In Germany, the ownership of coal and iron ore is vested in tbe State. The royalty paid on the former is 2 per cent, on the profits. At a selling price of 6s. per ton,the profit will be such that ltd. per ton will cover this payment. For iron ore noth- ing is paid for the right of working. No objection on the part of the owner of the soil is allowed to prevent the minerals on his property-being worked, such prohibition being rightly considered as incon- , sistent with the interests ot the nation. . _ _

lln the United Sates the ownership of the rainerals goes with that of the surface, and as coal and iron ore lands have bean, and still are, sold for a few pounds or even tlhillings per acre, the royal- ties ate neT4ii7 leas than in older countries? though by are frequently as high as in afly part of Europe. In Prance all ironstone save a trifling amount Whlch Oi an allnvial character, and all coal since 1810, have been claimed by the State. Concessions to applicants are granted on an annual payment of about Bs. per square kilometre (about 245 acres). In addition a tax is levied not exceeding &per tent. on the profits. If the latter amounted to 2s. per ton the royalty would be below lid. per ton. In Belgium before 1830, the iron ore was the pro- perty of the State, when it was transferred to the owners of the soil, by whom leases are granted on payrdent of from 41-d. to 2s. per ton. This reaction- ary step has been more harmful in the past than it Is now, owing to the fact that little iron is now worked, and the question of royalty is therefore comparatively an Culimportant one. Coal remains the property of the State.. The rent on it is Id. per Lnnum per hectare (a little above two acres), with 2;1 per cent. on the annual be profits. This, on an assume. 4 profit of 25.1 wonld under td. per ton. The minerals in Spain also bei:lng to the State, concessions being granted on nominlii terms. A comparison of the following chari;eB will suffi- ciently show hoiti. landlordism handicap the min- ing industry by the heavier tributes which it demands. The facts should be noted by land nationalisers who desire to strengthen their cage.• In Great Britain (under private ownership of minerals). Pig iron per ton, Cleveland, 35., Cumberland and Lancashire, 68. 3d„ Scotland, 3s. to 6s. On iron ship plates ss. 91. will represent a common charge for royalty; and 3s. Bd. to 78 3d. on steel rails, ac- cording to the ore from which they are made. In the United States (under private ownership). The Royalties vary from nothing (in rare cases) Itp to Cs. or Is. per ton:. .

THE STRIKE IN THE DIJIMAII COAL TRADE TERRIBLE DISTRESS. - - _

The miners in the eastern section of Durham, where the largest collieries are situated, still maintain a determination to resist the reduction of 14 per cent. on their wages demanded by the coalowners, and it is pretty certain the ballot of lodges will again result in a majority for a continuation of the strike,which is now in the 10th week, about 80,000 men being idle. Many lodges have voted in favour of a reduction ranging from 5 to 10 per cent. and to arbitrate on the remainder, and the Federation Board will probably endeavour to negotiate wi h the owners on such a basis at the next conference. Meanwhile the distress is very severe in the colliery dis- tricts and in Sunderland, where most of the coal is shipped. Several thousand men connected with the shipping and coal trades have been idle upwards of two months. Money is being subscribed for their support, but many families are slowly starving. The Durham Miners' Federation Board on Thursday issued a' circular advising the men to agree to 10 per cent, reduction, and asking for power to meet the owners with this offer. The lodges are requested to vote again on this proposal, letting the federation know the result:by Saturday neat.

div.head: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART. • THE PROPOSED TRANSFER TO THE CORPORATION. ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.
div.p: WARRINGTON SCHOOL OF ART. • THE PROPOSED TRANSFER TO THE CORPORATION. ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

On Thursday night a special meeting of the annual-subscribers and truateea of the above-named school was held in the Museum Lecture Room, for the purpose of considering, and if thought fit con- senting to, an arrangement transferring the school to the Corporation, under the provisions of the Schools for Science and Art Act, 1891. Mr. John Ryl ands presided, and was supported on the platform by Mr. P. Monks, Mr. R. F. Garnett, director of technical instruction of the Lancashire County Council, and Mr. W. Owen, secretary and treasurer of the Art School. Among those present there were also Messrs. C. S. Burgess, A. Chandley ; Mr. C. R , Aylward, head master of the school, and Messrs. John Hatton, C. Twist, Walton. Lees, and C. Madeley (librarian). The SECRETARY, at the request of the Chairman, read the notice convening the meeting. The Cmunrasti said before proposing the resolution he should like just to make a few, remarks to remind those present of something about the history of the School of Art. They had been in existence as a school for a good many years, and they had had to struggle sometimes. They had had some difficulty in carrying on, and yet somehow or other the result had been tolerably satisfac- tory. He might remind them that at any rate they had turned out some very good artists. One of these was certainly one of the cleverest artists of the day, Mr. Luke Fildes, and there was also his brother-in-law, Mr. E. Woods. Then there was Mr. Brewtuall, and there was poor Warrington Wood. In addition to that they had got results which, considering the size of the town and the school, would compare very favorably with much better schools elsewhere. The Chairman then read the following particulars pertaining to the history of the ' school. The class for drawing opened in 1850 at the Mechanics' Institute, was handed over to an indepen- dent committee as a School of Art in 1853, the teacher being Mr. Collinson, who left, for London school in October 1853. Mr. J. C. Thompson was recommended by the Department, and appointed master in October, 1855, resigning iu July, 1884. The Committee in 1853 was :—President and permanent Chairman of Committee, J. Wilson Patten, Esq., M.P., the Mayor, Peter Rylands, Esq., M.P., ,Rev. 11. Ros- tock, Rev, R. A. Mould, B. Pierpoint, Esq., M, Webster, S. Holden, S. Chandley, E. Brewtnall ; hon. secretary, Mr. E. Brewtnall,lBs3 to 1856; hon. treasurer, 1853 to 1856. Hon. treasurer 1866 to 1884. Treasurer, J. Rylands from 1856 to 1866. Mr. H. B. White, hon. secre- tary, 1888 to 1872. Mr. E. Milner, hon. secretary, 1872 to 1881. Mr. J. E. Ellison was hon. treasurer from 1884 to 1885, and now Mr. Owen was secretary and treasurer. (Applause.) The classes were held at Academy-place from 1853 to 1857, removed to Moseorn puildin,.s In 1857, and to the presgi4 HlNcli ii 2 iges. He was bound to say that ' outing his Connection with the School,of Irv. tie had had sonic very anxious moments. Be had , begun to despair of their ever being able to do what they wished to do. It was true they got a new school grant when really he thought it was impossible, and they got masters, and really had been tolerably pros- perous. But they had been short of funds, and had had difficulties in carrying out what they wished ; and there were lots of things they could have done if they had had money. This had made him very anxious that the school should be transferred to the Corporation. It was true that now the school was in a much better position than formerly, and could carry on fairly well without the assistance of the Corporation or any other body. But they were in much want of additional room, especi- ally for modelling. The evening classes were some- times mostly too crowded. The Corporation would with - their ample means be 0410 enlArge the school and pro- vide for trAching reienee, for technical education, and a ' variety of things far better than the present committee , could. Some of their friends had argued that because it was now in a much better position, the school ought no i to be transferred, but he looked to the future, and was i satisfied that the Comraittee could not do better than pet the school under the Corporation. He should have 1 great pleasure in :seeing I and be a , it handed over, having the full- est confidence that .it would be well managed,. great benefit to the town. The Chairman then pro- I ' posed the following ritk.slutaloOrof Art be transferred to "That the Warrington on on the following terms, the Corporation of Warresg. ke over the School subject viz. :—The Corporation to' ea. , contained in the deed of to the covenants and condititms. d Winmarleigh, dated conveyance of the site from Lot, 'lOOl trust deed dated 31st December, 1877, and in the Sea. to be executed to ,let May, 1883; a proper conveyanini 'on shall covenant the Corporation, in which the Corporalii, in whom the to indemnify the managers and trustee* 'ity in respect land and buildings are vested, from all HMI& II liability of covenants and conditions, and also &our a.. Govern- in respect of the building grant made by tihis school ment to the School, and further to carry on the , the at all times as an efficient School of Art :: anti of Corporation to execute and deliver a duplicaen such conveyance to the managers or trustees. The transfer to take place as from the first day of January, 1893, or such earlier day as may be agreed between the managers and the Corporation after the consent of the Science and Art Department is obtained, and the Corporation to take over the engagements of the managers with the teaching staff and other current expenses of the school as from the date of transfer,and the Corporation to pay all expenses in relation to the transfer. So long as the building grant made by the Department of Science and Art is not repaid to the Exchequer, the school buildings shall be devoted solely to the instruction of children and adults in drawing, painting, modelling, designing for architecture, manu- factures, and decoration ; and in the pure and natural sciences applicable to industry and manufactures. They shall be open at all times to the inspection of the officers of the Department of Science and Art. The students shall be instructed by teachers qualified to earn pay- ment from the department on the result of their teach- ing?,

- Mr. F. MONKS said he seconded the resolution, with very great satisfaction, because he believed that it was a step in the right direction in the interests of the school, and he endorsed the remarks that had fallen from Mr. Rylands. As to the future usefulness of the school that would depend upon the committee which had charge of it, and of course it primarly depended upon the inhabitants themselves as to whom they sent to the Town Council, because the Town Council had the ap- pointment of the committee. His friend, Mr. Rylands, had long had the idea that the school ought to be under the Corporation, but it was only recently that the way had been opened out through the action of the Govern- ment in giving to the County Councils a very large sum fof distribution throughout the county which had made it still more desirable that the transfer should be made. He expressed his earnest hope and belief that the trans- fer would be a most excellent thing for the school. By accident and not by design the director a technical education was over on a visit, and at his request re- mained that night and attended that meeting. . . .

The motion was put and carried unanimmly. Aylward, the head master, in his report stated: I have the pleasure to present a very satisfac- tory report on the work of the school of Art for the ; session endinr August 1891. The number of students 4 attending the classes exceeded any previous session. The total reached 265 ; the nreceding session closed with 239 • students. The comparative results on examination in 4 science drawing, including geometry, machine construe- , tion and building construction, are 58 successes 1891, as 4 against 46 1890. The first classes obtained in elementary art are-1891,35, as against 30 in 1810. In advanced , art the school has achieved distinction by students pass- ing in twelve subjects as compared with seven in 1890, resulting in 41 successes as against 30. In the advanced art perspective examination the paper worked by Stanley Pierpoint was marked excellent, being one of 65 so classed of 558 candidates. In the advanced art design examination John W. Dooley's paper was marked excel- ' lent, being one of 14 out of 607 candidates. John W. ' Dooley was selected by the Science and Art Depart- ment to attend the COMO on design at South Kensington, the department paying railway and i personal expenses. The marks awarded by the exam- iners of the department, and upon which Government -rant is paid, for works executed in the school. num- bei-ed 583, as against 319 in 1891. Seven of our students obtajned the award of full marks, against three in 1890. Of b 00.% prWes 23 were awarded of the value of 12s. each as Con:pared with five in 1690 ; and in addition five natiOtral book prizes, value 20s. each, were obtained anxf one national bronze medal was awarded to miss M. fL Kerry. Three free scholarships was granted by the Science and Art Department who pay all theft fees. Pull qualifying art master's certificates have been completed by Miss Annie airlines and Mr. Charles E. Jones. The school was successful in obtaining three art exhisttions out of eight offered by the Lancashire County Council, each the value of £ls,the successful candidates being Oswald Garside, Albert E. Hislop, and Herbert Woodier. Three students—Miss Mary Burgess, Miss Annie Chrimes, and Mr. J.tW. Dooley—have been again selected by the de- partment to attend the life class at South Kensington Schools during the month of .Tuly next, their expenses being defrayed. The department further recognised the work of the school by granting me permission to visit Venice during the summer vacatien of 1891, and fur- nishing me with such introductions to the managers of the Venice and Murano Glass Company as insured me a very gracious reception, and the full benefit of every explanation,as to the different prodesses of manufacture. I was also given by the company a complete set of their photographs, .which lihav'e exhibited in the school dur- ing the session.
The CHAIRMAN remarked that the report was unusually satisfactory, and very much to the credit of the head master, and he was very pleased be had been so suc- cessful.

div.head: LOSS OF 200 LIVES.
div.p: LOSS OF 200 LIVES.

Particulars have only just reached St. Petersburg of a terrible disaster, involving great loss of life, which occurred on the Caspian Sea at the end of March. As early as the 4th ult., a report was currant at Baku, and was telegraphed abroad, that a steamer had been wrecked while on a voyage to that port, but in the ab ence of further advices, the rumour remained unconfirmed. No doubt is now entertained, however, that the vessel referred to was the steamer Alexander Wolkow, which left one of the Persian ports on the southern side of the Caspian with goods and passengers for Baku at the end of March, and has never since been heard of. It is now practically certain that she foundered with all on board during a terrible storm which raged on March 29th. The precise number of lives Itst has not been ascertained, but it is known that some 200 Persians had taken pass- age for Baku, and all these were drowned beside the crew. How the disaster reallv occurred, however, can never be known, as everysoul on board perished.
