tens of thousands of acres of land in the United Kingdom that require draining; there is abund- ance of capital seekin.; an outlet ; but access to the land is barred by laws and customs which are a survival of the barbarism of the middle ages. The Liberals are pledged to reform these laws; the Tories make no pledger, for they know they mean to resist, as they have always resisted, any Proposal : which would take power from the aris- tocracy and give it to the people. As a part of the reform of the land laws the Liberals will have to deal with the iniquity of Mining Royalties. The Tories appear neither to 'know nor care anything about them, although every town in Lancashire—and Warrington in Particular—suffers grievously from the burden they impose. Mr. ROB SRT PIERPOINT is dumb; and Dr. RENTOUL, who came to enlighten every- body, had to confess, that be was absolutely ignorant ou that subject. A writer in a Tory contemporary .Puts a series of questions which show that he is Under the impression that it is the owner of land 'who pays Royalty and that he pays it to the State. What a gross delusion ! It is the owner of the land who himself fixes and receives the Royalty— money 'Paid for the privilege of getting minerals which ° ught to belong to the nation. In some cases more . actually paid to the landowner for permission t° get iron ore than is paid to the workmen *llO smelt it ! In Germany the ownership of coal and iron ore is vested in the State, with the re- sult that not more than 80. per ton of Royalty is charged upon steel rails, as compared with a ItoYalty of 7s. 34. per ton upon rails manufactured Nland. Need we be surprised that, under f ‘'neh circumstances, we suffer from the pressure c foreign competition ? Is it any wonder 'ha', We hear again and again of orders go- nag to the continent which have usually been ezecuted in this country ? Take the case of War- tington alone ; it is estimated that the black mail levied in the shape of Royal- ti. '4l upon the iron and steel manufactured In the town amounts annually to £50,000. In "many, or Franco, under State ownership, the PaYinent could not be more than £lO,OOO. It nal% therefore, be said that Warrington, as one tcll'u in the Kingdom, is being plundered every tear to the tune of £40,000 by landowners who "0 had no more to do with producing the minerals thwi the man in tho moon! The Tories arfess to know nothing of this; but, as the great jndowners, they pocket the money. Let work- consider these matters, and vote for I;arldidateB who will help to relieve them of these klirclens, and stimulate trade by removing the "a/Tiers to the progress of the nation.

Several letters, &e., are unavoidably held over until our next issue.

" Inquirer " may rest assured that the story is a story; it was born of envy and nurtured in malice. Mrs. Houston is the niece of Sir John Banks, the leading physician of Dublin. Dr. Houston is in Warrington, and will address two Meetings next week.

Lady Greenall presided, on Monday evening, as Ruling Councillor of the Daresbury Habitation of the Primrose League. It was stated the other day that she is not the writer of the " lame and impotent" verson of " What Paddy gave the Drum " which appeared in the" Observer." Very good ;we accept the statement. It is not for us to evade the issue, by saying we "don't care for squabbling with females." We leave it to the gentlemanly organ of " the party of gentlemen" to use such language, and to repeat false state- ments when there is a lady in the case.
What difference 'tween the "Observer" And our Ambassador at Rome? W by, only this—one "lies abroad " ; The other lies at home.
R. Pierpoint has a claim on us, And who shall say 'tis weak? He's had his" photo" taken abroad, And hob-nobbed with a Sheik.

It is amusing to observe how the Tories of War- rington are trying to get rid of the title they have earned as the Beer Party. Have they not for a generation supported a brewer as member of Parliament—a brewer who, by voting for compen- sation to brewers, was party to the project to plunder the people of this country of millions of money ? And who but Tory magistrates gave their consent to opening a vault in Ship Yard, and that, too, notwithstanding the strong ex- pression of opinion on the part of the Chief Con- stable?

Further: What about the Tory candidate? Has he not pledged himself to follow in the foot- steps of 'tit Gilbert Greenall ? He, too, is in favour of compensation to brewers; and he is, of course, opposed to placing power in the hands of the people to determine by a direct veto whether and what licensed houses they will have in their midst. The Boer Party indeed If it were not for the Beer Barrel, the Tories of Warrington would not have the ghost of a chance at the next election.

The replies which Mr. W. R,. Kennedy, Q.C., the Liberal candidate for St. Helens gave to the questions affecting the interests of railway servants were much more definite and satisfactory than those furnished by Mr. Seton-Karr, the Tory can- didate; but, notwithstanding this it has been re- solved by the local branch of the this, Servants Society to remain neutral so far as. the society is concerned. It seems that only fifteen persons were present at the meeting, on Sunday, and at least two-thirds of them were Tories. They couldn't say—" Vote for Mr. Kennedy," so they resolved to say nothing.

It is not at all an urcommon thing for Tory working-men t-) try to block the way when it is a question of deciding, in tho interests of working- men, between two candidates. The other week a few Tories at Warrington caused the Labour Council to stultify itself by declining to discuss the very issues raised at the Trades Congress. What is the use of agitating for reforms from year to year if, when the time for action arrives, nothing is to be done P

In our present issue, we give the answers which the Warrington railway servants have received from the Warrington candidates ; and the tale is the same : the Liberal candidate meets each issue, and meets it favovrably ; while the Tory candidate sends a letter in general terms,which do not:commit him to anything. Perhaps lie will give a more definite answer after the election.

However, the bulk of railway workers know what they are about, and will appreciate at its true worth a policy of evasion and delay. If they are true to themselves, they will vote Liberal, for they cannot but perceive that their only hope of shorter hours and redress of grievances lies with the Liberal party. A tree is known by its fruits, and the fruits of Toryism are the maintenance of the privileges of the classes as opposed to the rights of the masses.

Take a case in point : Lord Salisbury resigned office in 1866, rather than be party to an exten- sion of the franchise to working-men in towns, and in 1884 he brought the country to the verge of a revolution by resisting the extension of the franchise to labourers in the country. The Tories of to-day, as shown by their votes in the House of Commons on Wednesday, are opposed to the just principle of" one man one v6,te " ; and they scout the idea of payment of members, for they do not want to see the representatives of working- men in the House of Commons.

Still, everything with the Tories must be" Eng- lish, you know " ; but who is this " Schonberg K. McDonnell" who acts as private secretary to Lord Salisbury ? Is he a German or an Irishman, or a compound of both ? It would be all the better, very likely, if he were a bye-product of two nations; but as the name stands it doesn't look "English, you know." Dr. Rentoul, who poses as an authority on names, should be asked to give an account of the origin of "Schonberg K. McDonnell."

Lord Salisbury has expressed himself in favour of retaliatory duties. What if we were to retaliate upon the Australian colonies who are Protection- ist ? In 1873, Australian hides were from 6d. to Bd. per lb. To-day the same hides can be bought for from 2-id. to 3d. per lb. Still, the tanning trade is far from brisk ; but how would it be if the price of hides were artifically increased by an im- port duty ? It will be said that it is not intended to tax raw materials; but the principle is the elms, tax whatever we will ; and that is that thci tax is paid by the consumer. No addition to taxation will improve trade.

Mr. Gladstone has intimated to his election agent at Midlothian that in his opinion he will be called upon to appeal to the electors before the end of next month. This is, to say the least of it, significant. The decision as to the dissolution does not of course rest with the leader of the Liberal party; but even the Tory organs admit that his view of the situation is not to be taken lightly. Liberals cannot afford to neglect this warning from their chief ,• it means work, work, work, and yet again work; so that when the sum- mons to battle comes they will be able to say— " Ready, ay, ready." •

The Orangemen of Liverpool are being sat upon by the Constitutional Association. Seven of their number have been expelled for supporting an Orange candidate at the last Everton municipal election; and now the officers of the Orange Order threaten to withdraw all Orange representatives from the Constitutional Association. Puzzlo : To discover which is " Constitutional " and which isn't. By-the-bye when are the Orangemen of Warrington gfoing to make public the five ques- tions which, it is understood, they have submitted to the Tory candidate? And which of them is it that relates to the inspection of nunneries ?

More discussion as to the date of Warrington Walking Day. It is to be hoped the matter will be finally settled at the representative meeting which is to be held on Monday night next. Both Messrs. Pearson and Knowles and Messrs. Rylands Bros. suggest the first Friday in July (in preference to the fotirth Friday in June) as convenient for stocktaking—the half year being completed; and, unless there are serious difficulties in the way, the later date ought to be adopted.
The Runcorn Board of Guardians have under consideration the advisability of getting authority to hold Board elections every three years instead

div.head: EXAMTNER. SA TT) RDA Y, MAY 21, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMTNER. SA TT) RDA Y, MAY 21, 1892.

of annually as at present. But a greater change than that is needed; the whole system of election by open voting is utterly bad, and leads to corrup- tion and fraud. Then there are the property votes which swamp the votes of the working-class. The Liberals desire to change all this, but the Tories because they are Tories are doing all they can to uphold the existing order of things.

It seems impossible to write a novel now-a-days without giving a character a name which is iden- tical with that of some person in actual life. Mrs. Humphrey Ward has a "Paul Barbier" in her "History of David Grieve " ; and a Paul Barbier has written to say that the coincidence is calcu- lated to injure him. Mrs. Ward knew nothing of him when she wrote her story, and, as well as she can, sets him right before the public. But think of what might happen if a popular novelist were to give to a bad character the name of Smith!

Here is news which is good enough to be true: "The Daily Argus,' the Birmingham Liberal organ, authoritatively announces that Mr. Corrie Grant, the well-known barrister, will oppose Mr. Joseph Chamberlain in West Birmingham. Mr. Grant, according to the Argus,' intends to reside in the division and to conduct a very vigorous campaign. The announcement has created a great sensation in Birmingham, and has been re- ceived with the liveliest satisfaction by the Liberal party." Just so; Joseph is such a good fighter that it would be a pity to give him a walk over. Besides " Satan finds, &c."
PRNSENTATION TO A WIDNES FOOTBALLER.

In recognition of his services to football in Widnes, Mr. J. H. Smith, captain of the Widnes Football Club, was the recipient of a handsome gold keyless watch, on Wednesday evening. The presentation was made at Law's Railway Hotel, by Mr. Tom Smith, and Mr. A. Brown and Mr. Richards spoke of the valuable char- acter of Mr. Smith's interest in the club.—Mr. Smith suitably replied. A smoking concert was afterwards held.
PRITCRARD'S have now stood the test for 50 years,and quality and fir.t-elass work manship are still guaranteed.—Advt. MERSEY MISSION To SEAMEN, RUNCORN. _ . •

A concert was given in the Seamen's Institute, Run- corn, on Tuesday evening by about thirty girls,who were attired in sailor costume, and presented a charming ap- pearance. There was a good attendance of the seafaring class, who appeared to appreciate to the full the excellent programme of music. Miss Price and Miss Douglas gave a duet ; and Misses Rogers and Bancroft recited. A very young boat girl named Sarah Ri,gbv gave two recitations in capital style. A sketch entitled ." The stupid servant" caused much amusement. Mr. W. Shaw, the mission- ary, presided. If you want a lucky wedding ring go to 51. Ilton-sr.,where you will get a present with it.—Advt.
PIGEON SHOOTING M ATCH AT PANKITH.

On Mondiy afternoon a shooting match was held in Mr. W. Cooke's field, between George Kenwright and Tom Jackson, for 1.5 a side. The day was very windy,and interfered very much with the shooting. Jackson proved the winner, killing four birds out of five, while Kenwright missed all. Afterwards a sweep was shot off by the sportsmen on the field, the prizes being given by Mr. J. Jackson, of the Crown Hotel, ACE-BRAND S"ADES.—J. S. GARLAND, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrington. WARRINGTON HIGHWAY BOARD.

The first meeting of the new Board was held on Wednesday afternoon at the Masonic-room,Sankey- , street, Warrington, Mi. James Houghton in the chair. Captain Wallington was re-elected chair- man, Mr. W. Royston, vice-chairman, and Mr. James Houghton, junior vice-chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Henry Bate was elected a member of the Finance Committee. It was decided to con- tinue the improvement of Bennett's-lane, Cuerdly, and to request. Messrs. Sullivan and Co. to lengthen the approaches to the road. The Surveyor estim- ated the total expense of the ensuing year to be ..C4:125, which was equal to an 8(1 rate.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON. Sankey-t., Warrington.—Advt. BASE BALL.-WARRINGTON V. WIDNES.

The first match between the above clubs took place at Warrington, on Saturday, on the Sixpenny fields, Battersby-lane, before a large number of spectators. Mr. T. Gallop lost the toss, and Mr. Bates sent him in to bat. At the commencement the home team fared very badly, losing two men for one run, and it was not until A. Lingard, who played excellently for his 17, and J. Phcenix for his 9, that anything could be done with the fast bowl- ing of Keenekan: the innings closing eventually for the total of 40. Widnes then went in and scored 55 in grand style, their chief scorers being Keene- kan 8, and Waller 7. In the second innings the l'ome team worked hard for victory, and the good batting of the captain (T. Gallop) 10, J. Phcenix 10, W. Butterworth 10, J. Ashton 7, and G. Harding 6, making a total of 55. The second essay of Widnes only realised 37, leaving the home team victors by three runs; the grand totals being for two innings: Warrington, 93; Widnes, 92. After the match the teams adjourned to head-quarters, Cockhedge Mis- sion, where the visitors were entertained to tea. . .
, UMBRELLA RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-a.. Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN PRIM PUBLIC LIBRARY.
div.p: RUNCORN PRIM PUBLIC LIBRARY.

The Librarian (Mr. J. D. Jones) reported to Runcorn Free Public Library Committee on Wednesday that dur- ing the month of April there had been 1,930 volumes issued from the lending department, an increase of 23 on the corresponding month last year. 22 volumes were consulted in the reference department, a decrease of 17. The Committee had a balance in hand of £4B 14s. 6d. The Committee decided to expend £5O in the purchase of new books and to have about 60 old volumes rebound. Mr. Grice gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the library be open on one or more additional afternoons during each week for the convenience of borrowers. JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the hest stock- at ladles silver mut gold watches In the town.—. Advt. A TEMPERANCE FEDERATION FOR RUNCORN. A meeting of representatives of the various temper- ance societies and bands of hope in Runcorn has de- cided to form a Temperance Federation for the town and district. Amongst the functions of the Federation will be the consideration-of matters relating to licenses, and the taking of such action at the annual licensing session as may appear advisable. Concerted action is to be taken at the election of local administrative bodies ; and action will be taken by petition, public meetings, and otherwise in favour of licensing reform and temperance legislation generally. A Committee, whose duty is to draw up the constitution of the Federation, has been I appointed as follows :—Revs. C. Finch, J. Pulforcl Williams, Messrs. E. Wynae Humphreys, Posnett, D. Bisbrown, and T. Cooke. The last-named gentleman also acts as secretary pro -tens, and the Rev. C. Finch as treasurer.

JOSIIPH PRITCHARD'S sale shop is 51,11igh-st., his workshop 4, Bridge-st.—Advt FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT. Henry Anders, day wage man, living in Eccles- ton-st., St. Helens, was killed by the fall of a large stone in Ashton Green Colliery, St. Helens, at three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon. Another Elan narrowly escaped. JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- st., and 4, Bridge st., Runcorn.-44drt. A SUCCESSFUL CRICKETER.

The bowlers' competition organised by the" Sun- day Chronicle." was last week won by J. Harrison, of the Earlestown club, and lie becomes richer by one guinea. His achievement was in the match against Tyldesley on Saturday, the 7th inst., when he took seven wickets for five runs,with an analysis of 92 overs, 6 maidens, 5 runs, and 7 wickets.
Both PRITcaARD's Shops are under personal supervislomand customers may rely upon receiving every attention.—Alflet. A STURGEON CAPTURED AT WESTON POINT.

Last night week a sturgeon measuring 71t. 4in. in length, and weighing one cwt. and three quar- ters, was captured at Weston Point by son e divers employed on the Manchester Ship Canal works there. It was packed in a box and forwarded to the Royal Household at Windsor._ _

THE INCORPORATION OF WIDNES. On Wednesday morning Mr. 11. S. Oppenheim, clerk to Widnes LocaP Board, received a com- munication from the Home Office, intimating that the scheme of incorporation for Widnes had been approved b 3 the Privy Council, and asking for the usual tees to be paid. These were forwarded by the evening's post. It is expected that the charter will be to hand about the middle of June. The ap- proved scheme has previously appeared in these columns. UMBRELLAS lIECOVERED.—J. azd W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. A LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR KNUTSFORD.

Great interest will be excited in the Knutsford Parliamentary division by the announcement that Mr. A. M. Latham, son of the gentleman whose gallant struggle in Mid-Cheshire will be remember- ed, has agreed to come forward as the Liberal can- didate for the division. Mr. Thrutehley, who so largely reduced Lord Egerton's majority in the County Council election, had a strong claim on the Liberal party, but he has waived all personal con- siderations in favour of Mr. Latham. div.head: DROWNED IN A DOLLYTUB.
div.p: DROWNED IN A DOLLYTUB.

A sad drowning case occurred at St. Helens, on Thursday afternoon. While Mrs. Lowcock, wife of Alfred Lowcock, collier, of 6, Ileswell-st., was at- tending to her domestic duties, her daughter Elizabeth, 18 months old, rambled into the kitchen. A few minutes later, Mrs. Lowcock followed, and she then found that, by some means, the child had fallen into a dollytub, with her head in the wattif, which was about a foot deep. She immediately lifted the girl out, and it was then found that the unfortunate child was dead. SAFETY BICYCLES.-J. S. Garland, 51, Bridge-et., War- rington. See advertisement on page 4. . SERIOUS ACCIDENT TO A. ST. HELENS MAN. _ . _

At Barrow, on Wednesday week last, Thomas Reid, 20 years of age, son of Mr. Wm. Reid, of 55, Lyon-st., met with a very serious accident whilst following his usual employment in the shipyard. He was at work on a scaffold, when he fell and sus- tained a broken leg, two broken arms, and a brui. head. He was removed without delay to the hospi- tal, but mortification having set in it was found necessary to amputate his leg. The poor fellow lingers in a very critical condition. A FRANTIC WARRINGTONIAN AT RUNCORN. Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, David Plin- ston, of Warrington, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, at Halton, on the previous evening.—Superintendent Atherton stated that the prisoner was perfectly frantic, and it was impossible to lead or drise him.. It was necessary to take the horse from him and put it up at Wil- son's Hotel, at Runcorn. Subsequently P.C. Fryer apprehended the prisoner and conveyed him to the Police Station in a cart.—A fine of is. Gd. and costs was imposed, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment.

div.head: LORD CROSS AT SALFORD.
div.p: LORD CROSS AT SALFORD.

Viscount Cress, Secretary of State for India, was present at a meeting held in South Salford, on Thursday eveting, in support of the candidature of Mr. H. H. lloworth' M.P. In the course of his speech he asked tl4people of England to listen to the cry of the loyal people of the North of Ireland, and not to grant the establishment of a Parliament in Dublin. There were two nations in Ireland, and he believed that to maintain peace and a condition of prosperity the Imperial rule was necessary. It was the same in Ireland as in India, where Eng- land's paramount authority had created a condition of peace and happiness among a vast mass of people divided by race and creed. WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT HOMING SOCIRTY.

A very successful fly was brought off in connec- tion with the above society on Wednesday from Swindon, which is something like 121 miles away The first bird to arrive belonged to Mr. J. Buckley, having accomplished the journeY in a little over three hours, or at the rate of 1272 i yards per min- ute. Mr: L. Locker was second, third, and fourth, being close up with 1272 i velocity. The following were next ;—Mr. Barnes 1255 ; 6th, Mr. Greenough 1227 ; 7th, Mr. Greenough 1227 ; Bth, Mr. Burrows; 19th, Mr. Buckley; 10th, Mr. Buckley; 11th, Mr. Greenough ; 12th, Mr. Burrows; 13th, Mr. tiill ; 3 p.m. and Mr. Bracegirde 3.19. div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT RUNCORN, &c.
"By AN OCCASIONAL CORILIIISPONDENT."
That subscriptions do not flow in for the proposed Runcorn Technical Institute. So far as I can learn not one donation has been given since the appeal was issued.
That the formation of a Temperance Federation is highly approved in temperance circles in Runcorn and the new body is expected to do much good work in the cause.

That the conference of United Methodist Delegates of the Liverpool district at Runcorn this week, was a most harmonious gathering and the result of the facts disclosed and the discussions that took place should act for the benefit of the individual churches.

That should Mr. Cirice be successful in his endea- vour to get Runcorn Free Library open on one or two afternoons in the week besides Saturday. he will earn the gratitude of a large number of readers.

That there can hardly be any doubt that the rate- payers of Runcorn Union will express themselves in favour of a triennial election for Guardians at the poll which will be held to obtain their opinion.

That twelve months service is far too short for a man tobecome thoroughly acquainted wit') the affairs of the Union and the ins and outs of his duties as a Guardian and, leaving out of account the saving of expense that would accrue,triennial elections would be a great benefit.
That the system has been found to work well in the very large union of Prescot.

That the clause Mr. Brunner had inserted in the Local Government Bill, giving two or more autho- rities power to combine to prevent the pollution of ,reams in which they were jointly interested, has borne good fruit, and Mr. Brunner is to be con- gratulated on his foresight.

The Lancashire and Cheshire Councils have taken advantage of this clause to form a Joint Committee in respect to the pollution of the Mersey and lrwell and this Committee has now promoted a Bill in Parliament to obtain further powers to enable them to carry out their duties.

That the Chairman of the Police and Sanitary Regulations Committee of the House of Commons this week described the Bill as the most, important that had been before the Committee and gave per- mission for it to be taken before its turn.
That when this Committee get properly to work we may hope to see some water coming down the Mersey from Manchester way, and not a stream of stinking filth as at present is sadly too often the case.

That the teachers of Sunday Schools in Runcorn have had under consideration the question of Sun- day trading as it affects their work. That their attentits was drawn to the matter by the large numbers of children who purchased sweeth on their way to school, and the practice was denounced as likely to neutralise the good accomplished by the teachers, A resolution was proposed calling upon the various superintendents to urge the scholars to refrain from buying sweets on the Sabbath in future.
That I believe thess sweet shops are open at the same time as the public houses by virtue of a refresement license they hold for the purpose.
PROPOSED TRIENNIAL ELECTION OF
RUNCORN GUARDIANS.

At the fortnightly meeting of Runcorn Board of Guardians, on Tuesday, a letter was read from the Local Government Board in reply to the petition of the Authority asking that tho election of Guardians should be triennial iastead of yearly, as is the case at present. The Local Government Board advised that a poll should be taken to ascertain the feelings of the rate- payers, and stated that they were.prepared to grant an,. order directing that a will should be held, on application. It was also suggested to the Guardians that the feeling should be ascertained immediately, and not when a large number of the ratepayers were from home.—lt was stated that the cost of the poll would be £lso,but it was also explained that a triennial election would save the returning officer's tees, drc., for two years.—Mr. Hey- wood gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the Local Government Board be petitioned to allow of a poll being taken.
SHOCKING RESULT OF A BOYS' QUAMIEL AT WIDNES.

The Widnes Police on Wednesday apprehended a boy named Joseph Bowen, aged 13 years, who re- sides with his parents at 85, Midwood-et., on a charge of unlawfully wounding another boy named Harry Bratby, whose parents reside at 37, Gladstone-st., on the 10th inst. The injured boy's condition had become so serious that the police consid- ered it advisable to take his deposition which was done before Mr. Gossage, on Wednesday. The boy who appeared somewhat delirious, was sworn and said about 8 o'clock on the Tuesday evening named, he and some other boys were playing marbles in Milton-road, and the prisoner and some companions were throwing " sods." After a time the prisoner and his friends commenced to threw " sods" at those who were play- ing and Bratby chased and caught one ef them and thrashed him. He then went in pursuit of the prisoner, who fell down, and Bratby fell upon him, and he thought, hurt the prisoner's knee. He had got up from the ground and was walking back to his playmates, when he felt a blow on the back of his head. He was struck with a piece of slate or some solid substance, which cut through his pap and caused a wound which at once commenced to bleed. He went home and was attended by Dr. Allen, He had since been confined to bed.—ln reply to Mr. J. W. Knowles, who was pre- sent on behalf of the prisoner, witness said he could not tell who threw the stone or slate.—The prisoner was subsequently formally remanded.foi a week but was lib- erated on bail, his father in £4O and two sureties of £2O each.—The injured boy died from the effects of the wound, on Thursday at noon.

THE INQUEST. The inquest was held yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. F. A. Jones, the deputy coroner, and the proceedings occupied from 12 noon to 4 p.m., with an interval for lunch.—David Bratby deposed that the deceased was his son and was 16 years of age. He was apprenticed to a blacksmith. About ten witnesses mostly boys were called as to what took place in Milton- road, and while several said the stone which struck the

deceased came from the direction of the prisoner,others stated they saw the missile thrown.—Dr. Allen said he had made a post mortem examination and found the right lung very much consolidated which would itself cause death, bet in his opinion the lads death had been hastened by the blow on the head.—Mr. Knowles who appeared on behalf of the prisoner called Dr. Hudson who stated he was present at the post-mortem and he was of opinion that the lad had suffered from pneumonia and that the blow had nailing to do with his death.—'rhe jury after about ten minutes' delibera- tion in private, returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased died from pneumonia and inflammation of the lungs, accelerated by the blow he had received on the head from the prisoner Bowen. At the same time they found that the lad was not capable of knowing the wrong which he did.
STONE THROWING AT RAILWAY TRAINS AT RUNCORN. _ _ _

At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies, Thomas New- ton, aged 12 years,who lives with his parents in the Holloway, was charged with having on the 7th May maliciously thrown a stone at a certain carriage belonging to the London and North-Western Rail- way Co.. with intent to injure or endanger the safety of the persons then in such carriage.—Mr. Fenna (solicitors' department Lime-st.) prosecuted, and the defendant pleaded guilty.—Wm. Hickman paid he was a train reporter at Crewe station. On Saturday morning the 7th inst., when the 9-45 express trom Liverpool, arrived Mrs. Paton, of Sefton Park, Liverpool, who occupied a coupe compartment in the middle of the train, made a complaint to him. He saw that she had been injured under the eye and that the window of the carriage was broken. She handed the stone (produced a small boulder stone) to the station- mastee. The lady, who was on her way to Paris, jour- neyed to Manchester to consult a physician.—lnspector , Cooper said, acting under the instructions of Superin- tendent Atherton, he made inquiries about stone throw- ' ing on the railway. On approaching the house where the defendant resides, the boy saw tdin and commenced to scream and shout for his mother. That drew his (the Inspector's) attention to hitn, and he took him into the house. In reply to his inquiries the defendant said —" I threw a stone at the train with the intention of throwing it on the top of the carriage but it went through the window-" He made that statement in the presence of his mother and P.C. Worth. The defendant further stated that no other boys were concerned—" I done it myself."—Mr. Fenna said the punishment for this offence was very serious, but he did not wish that punishment to be inflicted upon this little boy. Under the Summary Jurisdiction Act the Bench had power to birch him, and he asked them to take that course. The Company wished to put a stop to this practice of stone throwing.—Mr. Brundrit, addressing the boy, said he might think at the time that it was a lark to throw stones, but he must be made aware of the gravity of the offence. He would receive 12 strokes with the birch rod, and let it be a warning to him and others. The Bench instructed P.S. Woolley to adminis- ter the strokes.

has been confined to his bed since last Saturda' y with an attack of bronchitis and inflammation of the lungs, but we are glad to say he is now convalescent, and hopes soon to resume duty.
JOSEPH PRITCHARD, Watchmaker and Jeweller, 51, High- et., 'Ltd 4, Bridge-It., Runeorn.—Adri. ST. JOHN'S BAND. OF HOPE, RUNCORN.
The members had their annual trip on Saturday, when a pleasant afternoon wes spent on Overton Hills, Frodsham. In the course of the day the officers and workers were photographed by Mr. floxworth.
QUICK DESPATCH AT RUNCORN DOCKS..

The steamer Fairport arrived at Runcorn Docks on Sunday, with 409 tons of flint on board,and commenced to discharge at midnight. The whole of the cargo was removed by 11-30 on Monday morning, and the vesel departed by that day's tide.
Go to PalioßlßD's for the best five gutuca watch a work- higatea can have.—.6ldet. GOIPEL UNION MISSION, RUNCORN. -

In connection with this mission, Mr. Richard Weaver, the well-known evangelist, preached two sermons in Runcorn Public Hall on Sunday last. There were good congregations. On Monday evening Mr. Weaver delivered a lecture descriptive of his life and labours. Collections were taken in aid of the mission funds. MILL BROW SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.

The anniversary sermons were preached in Halton-road Chapel on Sunday by the Rev. Alfred Sargent, of Wolver- hampton, who was in the Runcorn circuit 14 years ago. The sacred edifice was crowded at the evening service. The collections realised £26. In the school were 21 officers and teachers and 368 scholars, of whom 297 are members of the band of hope. Josiru PRITCIARD is prepared to wind and keep in repair private eloeke from 10s. per annum.—Adet. NEGLECT OF FAMILY AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Mr. A. Thomas, Wm. Parsons, was charged with neglecting his wife and four children, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Union. 'rhe prisoner, who had been apprehended at Pontypridd, by P.C. Bullock, pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to a month's hard labour. It was stated that his family had received relief to the extent of £6, JOB MPG( PRITCHARD keeps spectacle: to sMt all sights from a shilling a pair.—Advt. BRUNSWICK RAMBLING CLUB RUNCORN.

The members of the Rambling club in connection with Brunswick Improvement Class had their first " jaunt " on Saturday, when a party of about 35 paid a visit to Fox Hill, Frodsham, the residence of Mr. Jas. Reynolds, J.P., who had placed the grounds at their disposal. Afterwards tea was partaken of at Mersey View. The outing was much enjoyed. If you want your watch repaired by skilful workmen. take It to PAlTCRAiD'fi.—Ailvt.

PEERS ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY, RUNCORN. The third annual meeting of this society was herd on Friday night last, under the presidency of Mr. J. J. Speakman, who stated that the society was making steady progress. Last year they closed with a deficit of £65 18s. lid., and while they could not now show a credit balance, the debt had been reduced to £27 4s. Od. The Chairman described the advantages the society offered, and urged the members to individual effort in securing the society its full complement of 400 members. —The balance sheet and report were adopted, and the retiring directors, Messrs. T. H. Annett, G. H. Danbv, R. Morris, and S. Stubbs, were re-elected. Mr. J. W. Tickle was xe-elected members' auditor.

div.head: DRUNKEN SAILOR AND THE CIGARS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A DRUNKEN SAILOR AND THE CIGARS AT RUNCORN.

A seaman named Daniel Smith, was brought up at the Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Messrs. Brundrit and Handley, on a charge of stealing 80 cigars, value 10s., the property of Mary Ann McCammon, man- ageress of the Holyhead Harbour Beerhouse, High-st., en the 11th inst. About eleven o'clock on Wednesday night, the prisoner was in the vault, and was seen by Alice Conway, servant, to reach over the counter, and take a box of cigars off the slielf. She told her mistress, who put her hand in his pocket and took out several cigars, which were broken. She threatened to have him locked up, when he promised to show her where they were. She accompanied him to an entry in Regent-st., where she got about 30 more cigars. He said he would pay for the damaged ones on Friday.—P.C. Pettingale apprehended the prisoner under a warrant, on a vessel in the docks.—ln reply to the charge he said "1 have nothing to say; I was drunk at the time I took them." He was fined 303. including costs, or a month's imprison- ment.

ASSAULT ON AN INFANT STEPDAUGHTER AT RUNCORN. Henry Spencer, a young man, was summoned to Run- corn Petty Sessions•on Monday at the instance of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Chil- dren, for assaulting his stepchild, Fanny Mannering, aged three fears.—Mary Jane Plant, of Penketh Lahe, a married woman, said the defendant and her family lived with her. The defendant and the girl went to bed early, and between seven and eight o'clock, she heard a scream, and a bump en the floor, and she heard defen- dant say "Come on you young--and get into bed." Next morning the child appeared to have been whipped. —Dr. Mc Dougall said the Inspector of the Society brought the child to him on the 3rd May. She had two deep weals on each loin and a bruise on the right but- tock three inches in diameter. She had also bruises on the leg. Considerable violence must have used.—The defendant said he was as innocent as a babe unborn of assaulting the child. She fell out of bed trying to get out of bed over his feet and she dropped on his box and then on to the floor.—ln reply 0 the magistrates, Dr. McDougall said the bruises might have been caused by a fall, but the weals could be produced by nothing but a direct blow.—The defendant was fined ss. and "costs 103. 6d

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were present—Messrs. J. Knowles (in the chair), J. Whit- low, H. E. Heywood, J. M. Williams, J. Baguley, J. Brandretb, T. J. Weir, P. Hall, J. L. Jones, E. Bretherton, Joseph Baguley, W. Wilkinson, E. Aaron, C. Mounfield, and the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: HELSBY SEWERAGE.
div.p: THE HELSBY SEWERAGE.

Mr. Farrington, inspector of nuisances, reported that a meeting d the Helsby Local Committee had been held to consider the letter received from the Local Gov- ernment Board in reference to the drainage of Ilelsby. It was proposed by Mr. J. Jeffs, snonded by Mr- J. Ellams,that the open sewers in Mr. Thornley's garden be piped under with 15in. pipes, that a catch pit or cesspool be constructed thereto, and that the outfall sewer ditches be cleansed by the Sanitary Authority, when required ; also that the drainage of Ebenezer- terrace be intercepted into the present main sewer, if the levels admitted. It was also recommended that a ventilator be fixed thereto, and that the houses on the line of the said sewer be connected.

The Clerk suggested that the report be forwarded to the Local Government Board, and also that a copy be sent to Mr. Thor!:ley. This suggestion was agreed to, and Mr. Farrington was instructed to prepare specifica- tions of the probable cost ot the works.

div.head: S. MURTON REATH WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: S. MURTON REATH WATER SUPPLY.

The Clerk read a communication from Mr. Ross, Water Office, Warrington Corporation, under date May 2nd, 1892, informing the Authority that the Corporation were ! able and willing to supply water sufficient for domestic ' purposes within Corporation limits. He wished the Board to understand that the Corporation would not be bound at any time to lay on a supply of water without the limits of the borough, except that afforded by the pipes of the Corporation communicating with the sur- face reservoir. Continuing, the Clerk said that he for- warded a copy of the letter to Mr. R. Davies, who, he said, had displayed considerable interest in the subject, and he had received a reply that the saving clauss rendered the conditions useless, so far as those who resided on the south side of the Bridgewater Canal were concerned.—Mr. Farrington said that the pressure at the point where Mr. Davies resided was limited. It was agreed that Mr. Davks's letter be referred to Mr. Ross.
VIE STOCITON HEAT!! SEWIRAGE.

It was agreed on the motion of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Whitlow, that Mr. P. Silcock prepare a scheme for the sewering of Stockton Heath, and forward the plans to the Local Government Board for their approval.

div.head: RUNCORN YOUNU MAN'S ADVENTURE
div.p: A RUNCORN YOUNU MAN'S ADVENTURE
AT WIDNES.

Joseph Rowley, James-st., and John Hooligan, Pitt-St., were charged at the Widnes Police Court, on, Monday, before Messrd. Stapleton Bretherton and J. Lister, with stealing .£6 from George Thom- son, Greenway-road, Runcorn, and using personal violence at the same time. Mr. Knowles appeared for the defendants. George Thompson said he was in the Ivy. Green beerhouse, on Friday night, when the two prisoners came in. They had three drinks each. Witness then asked him if they could recommend him to any lodgings. 'rhey told him to go with them, and they would find a place. They all left together, and when they had got a shcrt distance Hooligan said "You cow, you have come far enough." He then struck him on the forehead and kn3cked him down. Rowley fell on his legs, and Hooligan on his chest. Witness felt one of the hands of one of the prisoners in his pocket. He had Le in his possession. After struggling, witness got up and ran into the main road. He was sure the two prisoners were the same men. He was sober at the time.—Cross- examined by Mr. Knowles : He had been to Chester Races on Wednesday and Thursday. He betted freely on a number of races, and won about £5 10s. He put £6 in his waistcoat pocket at Chester, and he had that amount on Friday evening, when coming to Widnes, but he had not seen the money since. Confirmatory evidence was given by Edith Rogers Annie Yearsley, employed at the Ivy Green, Ed. Bibby' night foreman at the works of the Liverpool Silver and Copper Coy. and P.C. Wood. George Dowers, storekeeper at the Copper Works, said he paid Rowley LI 11.. on Friday night and Hooli- gan £1 es. for their wages. On Saturnay morning Row- ley asked him for his S' check." Witness told him to go home, as he was not in a fit state to have his check, and further told him that he believed he was concerned in an affair on the previous night. He replied" How do you know ?" and then asked him for his We money, as he wanted to clear out of the town. Mrs. Rowley, mother of the prisoner Rowley, said her son paid her Ll ss. on Friday evening. He always gave her the greater portion of his wages. Charles Edworthy, Wareing-et., Widoes, barman at the Waterloo Vaults, said the two prisoners came into the vaults in company with three other men on Saturday morning, and called for some drink, for which Rowley tendered a sovereign, and said, '6 Them is the sort for Saturday morning." P.C. Evans proved apprehending Rowley on Saturday morning. He took him to the police station, and charg- ed him in company with Hooligan. Rowley replied "Good enough, I wish I had £6." Hooligan replied" I am not guilty of that. P.S. McGregor deposed that at the police station Hooligan made a statements, to the effect that Thompson paid for a drink for himself and Rowley at the Ivy Green on Friday night. They all left together, about half-past ten, and went towards the Copper Works. When they had got a little way, Thompson said " Lam off to my lodge," and cleared off. They did not see him again until all the men in the copper yard were brought together by Bibby, but Thompson did not recognize them. Mr. Knowles contended, for the defence, that there was no evidence to prove that the prisoners had robbed the prosecutor. Their worships, however, considered that there was a prima fade case against the prisoners, who were committed to take their trial at the nest Liverpool Assizes. bail being allowed.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

sEnnes or UNSOUND Fun.—An important seizure of upwards of fifty uasound mackerel was made at Prod sham in the Main-street, early on Monday morning. by Mr. Farrington, the Sanitary Authority inspeetor. He called in a Justice of the peace, who pronounced them to be quite unfit for human food and the inspector had the whole ouantity destroyed. The fish were in the possession pf a hawker.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WA ItRINGTON.

Mr. T. A. Dickson, M.P., who knows Ireland well and sits for an Irish constituency, will deal at the Co-operative Hall, on Monday night, with some of Dr. Itentoufs 'fax "—that is to say it there are any of Dr. Rentoul's patent facts left to deal with, see- ing that since this Doctor from Down was on his pilgrimage one or another of his statements has been flatly contradicted almost every other day. Mr. Dickson is a linen manutacturer and merchant of Belfast and sits for the St. Stephen's Green division of Dublin. lie sat for Dungannon from 1874 to 1880, and for Tyrone from 1881 to 1885.

Mr. Thomas Burt, who speaks at the Liberal meeting on Tue,day evening in the Empire Theatre is a Labour member of Parliament in the strictest sense of the word. Ile represents a constituency, Storpeth in Northumberland, in which the vote of the miners is dominant; he has been a working, miner himself; and he was selected and returned to. Parliament by miners,"to represent their interests. Mr. Burt was born something like fifty-five years. ago in a cottage adjoining the coal line which runs. from Backworth to the JNorthumberland Docks at North Bhields, and he worked in the mines at aa early age., lie sprang into prominence by the active - and sagacious part lie played in the strike of his. fellow miners at Cramlington in 1866, and be was- elected to Parliament in 1874, since when he has. retained his seat without opposition. The poll of 1874 gives a conclusive reason for this quiescence on the part of the Tories. It was as follows :—Burt,, 3,332, Duncan (C) 585.

There is a diminutive and unpretentious publica- tion in Warrington which is edited by a Tory. though not supposed to take any definite stand in politics, and which is known by a title suggestive of morning light. I understand that the editor is about to get up a sort of political census among his readers, with a view of ascertaining whether the majority of them are identical with himself in their views on Parliamentary matters. Some time ago a similar plesbiscite was taken in connection with the same paper, and the result of it was to be duly published therein, but I understand that when it came it showed such a considerable majority for Liberalism, that the editor thought silence would be decidedly golden in this case and did not publish the unpalatable return.

I see the Warrington Tories have been busy pamphleteering of late, and they have been circu- lating among the working-men a printed statement which is about as misleading and as lying a con- coction as could be manufactured to gull and bamboozle that class. They print in parallel columns lists of measures passed by the Tory and the Liberal parties respectively, solely or mainly in the interests of the working-classes, during the period from 1874 to 1891. Now—could it have been believed ?-1 myself can call to mind no fewer than 12 Liberal measures of that period which are entirely omitted in this mendacious pamphlet, in order that it may be made to appear that tAe Thries have passed so many more Acts for the benefit of the working class than the Liberals have.

Absolutely they have bad the unconscionable- ness to omit the County Franchise Act, that great measure which conferred the Parliamentary vote on the downtrodden agricultural labourer. I will enumerate the other measures:—The Patent Act, the Savings Bank Act, the Friendly Societies Act, the Allotments Extension Act, the Merchant Sea- men's Wages Act, the Safe Carriage of Grain Act, the Alkali Acts, the Extension of Hours of Polling Act, Abolition oh flogging in the army and navy,and the Diseases Prevention (London) Act. But this list with a little research could be considerably extended.

But even supposing that the Conservatives could cite more measures passed by them for the work- ing-men, the matter is not one to be determined numerically merely, but morally also. The County Franchise Act, I say, was worth in vital and far- reaching importance all the measures credited in the pamphlet to the Tories; you do not find them ever carry ing out such a reform as that.

They claim credit for the extension of the suffrage of 1867, but, as I recently showed, the Bill, though passed in a Conservative Parliament, was really a Liberal measure. And some of the measures claimed by the Warrington Conservatives for their party in the pamphlet might fairly be transferred to the i other side of the account, because only conceded by the Tories under extreme Liberal pressure in the House of Commons. They put down Free Education as one of the Tory measures, whereas the fact is that it was not given by the Tories, since one half of them voted against the second reading of the Bill, and it became law only through the votes of the Liberals, who would have made it a much better Act than it was, if the Tories would have allowed them in the voting on amendments.

Then again, there is another fact to be considered. During the period 74 to 91 the Tories have been in office over eleven years, while the Liberals have only heldpower.for some five years, though this fact is not i mentioned in the Tory pamphlet. And the Tories have been n office during the latter part of the period, when it has been easier to pass mea- sures for the benefit of the working classes than in the earlier period from 1880 to 1885, when public and Parliamentary opinion was not so advanced. But bad the Liberals been in the ascendant during the eleven years the Conservatives have been, since 1874, what would the Liberal record not have been? And since that popular opinion which makes reform i practicable advances as time advances, it s not fair I'to take even the splendid Liberal record of the past as a complete criterion of what it will be in the future. It is by the light of considerations like these that the Warrington working-men must esti- mate the value of the Tory pamphlet; which is about as unqualified a hotch-potch of untruthful— ness, direct and indirect, as could have been com- pounded.

At last the people of Earlestown have surmounted the imaginary obstacles which they considered blocked the way, and have instituted a May Queen festival. As if to smile encouragement upon their efforts, " Old Sol" was on his best behaviour, arid ,shone forth brilliantly the whole of the day, in fact everything, atmospherically, was in favour of success, and from what I hear the financial part of the undertaking was perfectly satisfactory. As a maiden effort,l congratulate the promoters heartily upon the magnificence of the turn out, and I think the parents of the children deserve every praise for the interest they manifested in the enjoyment tbe youngsters extracted from the affair. Such displays are purely incidental to the children, and there cannot be any doubt that each one felt hd played the most important part in Saturday's' de- monstration. Great things are promised for next year, and I only hope that the inhabitants will co-operate in as hearty a manner as they did on Saturday.

There was quite a scare in some quarters in Newton the °tiler night. It will be remembered that, last week, the foundation stone of the exten- sion of St. Peter's Church was laid by Col. AlcCor- quodale, and beneath the stone was placed a bottle contsming a number of coins. A policeman going his rounds, a night or two alter, found an iroit bar lying near the stone, and the assumption Was that some impecunious person bad been making an attempt to become possessed of the bottle of coins, but that he had been disturbed by the app-oach of te guardian of the people's property. Inquiry next morning, however, showed that the bar had been left there by the workmen inadvertently. Nevertheless the temptation to anyone so inclined was great, and the facilities for enriching them- selvest;in'ld at easy reach; thus the sooner they MERLIN. upon the stone, the better it will be for the bottle.

It was decided on Saturday, at the Unionist meeting at Gloucester, that Mr. Colchester Wemyss should oppose Sir Charles Dilke in the Forest of Dean Division. In a letter to his election agent in Midlothian, Mr. Gladstone says that before the end of next month be will again ask the electors for their vote of conedence. A revolver has been turned upbv the pleugh in a field over which the burglar Peace is known to have taken flight after shooting Mr. Dyson at Banner Cross, Sheffi- eld. . descendant oil Sir Walter Scott, Father William Lockhart, who was also the first of the Oxford Tracta- rian converts, waslfound dead in bed on Sunday morn- ing. At Buckingham Palace, on Monday afternoon the Princess Christian held the first Drawing-room of the season, on behalf of the Queen. There was a large attendance.

It is stated that the Glasgow shipowners, in conse- quence of the depression in the shipping trade, are con- sidering the advisability of laying up one-third of theit vessels for a time, and asking others to join with. them.

div.p: • QUININE BITTERS-NOTHING MORE. • Once upon a midnight dreary, ill in bed quite weak and weary With sleeplessness, lone spirits, and indigestion sore ; While I strove in vain at napping, suddenly there came a tapping, As of some one gently rapping—rapping at my chamber door!
" It;^s-Doetor Draughts," I muttered. ber door."
"tapping at my eliam

'Twas the Doctor, nothing more. Oh I distin3tly I remember ; it was in the bleak December, And in every single member of my body pains I bore. Eagerly I wished the morrow, vainly had I sought to borrow From drugs surcease of sorrow—sorrow for my pains. g 'lore ; And I &eked if I should ever be as healthy as before. Quoth the Doctor. " Nevermore I" " Your chest is bad, that's certain; your neuralgia's always
hurting, And your4liver is so sluggish firth, life's to you a bore; And your heart's so bad at beating that in vain you're sleep

THEFTS. At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Monday, Alice Skeeley, last from Widnes, and newly out of prison, was charged with stealing, on the night of the 12th inst, a metal watch and chain, value 55., the property of Robert Daniels. The prisoner had come to the prosecu- tor's house and asked to be allowed to stay the night there, and had taken advantage of her being there to carry off the watch and chains She was apprehended at Widnes. The prisoner was committed to jail for a month.—At Monday's Court also John Price, last from Chester, was charged with stealing, some time between 11 p.m. on the 14th inst, and 8 a.m. on the 15th inst, ss. in cash, the property of Alfred Talbot, 37, Scotland-rd. The prisoner was apprehended with the money in a handherchief which he had round his foot. Re was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.

THEFT OF A COAT. Catherine MacDonald, wife of Patrick MacDonald, forgeman, living in Dallam-lane, was charged on Mon- day, at the Warrington Police Court, with stealing on the 7th inst., a black worsted coat, the property of Thomas Rooney, a labourer at Dallam Forge, residing at 43, Watkin-st., or receiving the same, knowing it to have been stolen. The complainant had sent a child to take the coat out of pledge at Tunstall's in Winwick-st., and while it was being redeemed it disappeared. Detec- tive-Sergeant Monaghan found that it had been pledged on the 9th inst., at Jackson's in Winwick-st., by a boy named James Mahony, and he saw the prisoner, who told him she had sent her little boy with same bundles to Tunstall's and he brought the coat back. She was ping to return it, but on the advice of a woman had it pawned for her.—The prisoner was fined 205., including costs.

div.head: THEFT OF CLOTH _BY A WOMAN..
div.p: THEFT OF CLOTH _BY A WOMAN..

-- At the Warrington Borough Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday, Mary Cokeley. wife of John Cokeley, labourer, 8, Tilley-st., was charged with stealing, on the previous afternoon, a roll of cloth, containing twenty yards of material, the property of Fowler Bros., drapers, Butter- market-st. A little girl saw the prisoner come out of the shop with the cloth, and informed the prosecutors. They acquainted P.C. Meacock, and be and P.S. Cheney went to the prisoner's borne, and found her there, and a quantity of cloth under the bed of the sofa. They took. it to Messrs. Fowler' and it was identified' as theirs, but two yards were still wanting. It was ascertained that two yards of cloth had been offered in pledge at Jack- son's pawnshop. These were afterwards found under the bed of the sofa at the prisoner's home, though they had not been there at first, and they proved to be the missing two yards. The prisoner at home denied her guilt, but at the Station, in reply to the charge, said she had "nowt to say.'!—She was fined 14., including costs..

A JUVENILE PIGEON STEALER. At Monday's Warrington Police Court, charges were preferred against a youth aged 17, named William Broderick, who had been three years in an Industrial School, of stealing, en the night of the 7th lust, four pigeons, the property of Alexander Baird, of the Crown Inn Beerhouse, Queen-st., also with stealing, on the 16th . lust, four more, the property of the same complainant. Be sold the first two birds to a person in Mill-st., on the night of the 16th, and came back with two others to sell, when he was detained on suspicion, and handed over to the police.—The lad said hls father had run away, and he could not get wnrk.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner did not know one night where he would lodge the next.—Mr. R. Garnett, who was presiding, said these cases came on, and these lads said they could not get work, but there was a great difficulty in getting lads, and there were lots of farmers who would give them 6s. a week if they would work, but they would rather loaf about the town and carry a parcel for 6d.— The Bench let the prisoner off with a mere record of his conviction. TEE JUVENILE MAEIiET THIEF AGAIN. Percy Quinn, a lad, was brought up at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing, some time between 11 p.m. on the 14th, and 8.30 a.m. on the 15th a quantity of sweets, value is., the property of Joseph Lawless, Market Place.—Mr. Plaice, the Market Inspector, said a short time ago the prisoner was found by Mr. Lawless hidden on his premises, and he got away. Afterwards he was brought up with three or four other boys on the charge of robbing a shop, in the Market Htll, and was dealt with leniently. On Saturday night he came into the Market &at, and con- cealed himself in the cellar until the Market Hall keeper had closed up. He lit a fire in the cellar, and e joyed himself with the stolen sweets,and some biscuits. That morning the prisoner had been found by the keeper con- cealed in a shop near the Market Hall door, so that if he was not found be might slip out as soon as the door was cpened.—Evidence as to the disappearance of the stolen articles, and the damage of others, was given.—Mr. Plaice said the lad stated that his father had not given him anything to eat.—He was ordered to be sent to the Workhouse. AUDACIOUS THEFT OF A CONCERTINA.—THE INSTRUMEN'T

div.head: FOUND IN ST. HELENS CANAL . _
div.p: FOUND IN ST. HELENS CANAL . _

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednes- day Isaac Smith, a glass works labourer, formerly of Warrington, but latterly of St. Helens was charged with stealing at Bank Quay station early on Sunday morning a mahogany box containing a concertina, the property of Robert Hannan, of Manchester. The Chief Constable stated that Hannan arrived on Saturday night at the . station by the 11.20 p.m. train, but missed a train he wanted to catch there, and had to wait for the 2.30 train on Sunday morning. About midnight, the prisoner, accompanied by a man named George Rhodes, came to the station, and remained sitting there till about one o'clock. He then got up and snatched the. box containing the concertina, and ran out of the station. The complainant and Rhodes went to- gether and reported the matter to P.C. Fleetwood and at the police station.—P.S. Monaghan appre- hended the prisoner on Sunday at St. Helens, and brought him to Warrington, and then went back to his residence 10, Potter-st. Green Bank, St. Helens, to inquire about the concerana. The prisoner's wife was at Warrington, but a little girl was in the house and pointed out to Monaghan where her mother had thrown the concertina into the canal. He dragged for it, and, after much trouble, discovered the remains of it in a bag among some bricks or stones. The prisoner afterwards said he had left the concertio t home on a shelf. The St. Helens police were not in the habit of looking for lost articles as the Warrington police were, or the concertina would have been recovered safe and sound.— The prisoner pleaded guilty, but said he was very sorry; he had had a drop of beer.—P.C. Fleetwood said the man was sober at the time.—He was sentenced to a month's imprisoment with hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SextranAg.---Before Alderman Burgess, Mr. Lewis Voisey, and Mr. J. Geddes. A FIT SUBJECT FOR RAINRILL.--JaMeS Fidler was ,charged with acting in a disorderly manner in sankey- st. at 10-0 on Friday night.—lt appears that the pri- soner entered an omnibus at Sankey Bridges, and on its arrival in Sankey-et. he was found lying on the floor in a nude condition. A constable endeavoured to dress 1, Lim, and had partially succeeded, when the prisoner 02Eoke away and ran up the street. His arrest was

effected, and it was necessary to convey him to the Bridewell. Since his arrest the prisoner had displayed symptoms of lunacy, and he was ordered to be detained in the Workhouse.—The prisoner was then removed, shrieking at the top of his voice. —At the close of the court, Dr. Peacocke expressed an opinion that the man was a fit subject for removal to Rainhill Asylum. AN EXACTING TRAMP.—John Warren, a tramp, was charged with disorderly behaviour in the werkhouse, and doing damage to the extent of one shilling.—Mr. Ward, the master of the workhouse, stated that the prisoner was on the No. 4 diet, which comprised a pint of milk in the morning and a pint of milk in the even- ing, with ten ounces of tread and rice pudding. On Thursday morning the prisoner was served with a cer- tain amount of bread, but minus the milk, as that did I not arrive until nine o'clock. The prisoner demanded the milk at once, and because he could not be served, he went into a violent temper, and threatened to cut his throat, the nurse's, and several other people's. Re threw the tin down the stairs, and the bread at the attendant who served him with it. The prisoner, who made use of several unbecoming expressions in court, was sentenced

to 21 days' hard la-hour. DEFRAUDING A RAILWAY Co.—A man named William Wilding was charged with travelling from Widnes to Warrington, on the London and North-western Railway; without a ticket, and also with being drunk and dis- orderly on Friday night. Holland, the ticket collector, said the prisoner came off the train on Friday night, and presented a ticket from Liverpool to Widnes. He refused to pay the fare from Widnes to Warrington, say- ing that he was overcarried, owing to being asleep when the train stopped at Widnes. Prisoner was also drunk. The magistrates fined prisoner ss. and costs. Moon:ay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, and Francomh. WIFE ASSAULT.-- William Caldwell Ness charged with assaulting his wife, Martha Elizabeth Caldwell, on the 13th inst.—The complainant said the defendant, when drunk, struck her about the head and face with the buckle of his belt, and as she lay in bed, stood upon her with a paraffin lamp, threatening to throw it over her. Be was enraged -because she would not give him money for drink. She had had two separation orders from him, but had forgiven him .—He denied the charge, but was sent for three months' hard labour. / CRUELTY TO A Hoasn.—Wm. Smith, living at a lodg- ing-house in Waerington, was charged with cruelly, ill- treating a horse by overworking it. Inspector Dowty,„ R.S.P.C.A., and other witnesses proved the case, Mr. Dowty stating that the animal had the appearance of being both overworked and underfed. The defendant was fined 20s. and costs, in default 14 days imprison - ment. IN THE MARKET FOR FELONIOUS PIIRFOSES.—Wrn. Keith, a Londoner, was charged with having been found in the Market Hall, at one o'clock on Sunday morning for felonious purposes. A constable found him hidden under a stall. The prisoner said he was there be- cause he could not get lodgidgs. Fined 35., the amount he had in his pocket, or 7 days. CHILD DESERTION.—John Leach, tailor, was charged under a warrant, by Mr. B. Shearer. on behalf of the Guardians, with leaving his child chargeable to the Union. He had put it to a cost of £8 4s. He was sent to jail for a month's hard labour. Diatront.—Wm. Fitzpatrick charged with being drunk in Scotland-road, dismissed with a caution.—Alice Keavan in Sankey-st., dismissed. DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—RaIph Wood, on the 9th of July, 1891, 10s.—Nancy Swarbrick was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Arpley Bridge, on Satur- day night. She was quite incapable and had to be taken to the station in a handcart.—She had to pay the lock- up fee, 2s. ; Charles Brown, in Rose and Crown-st.. he having been fighting with a man for, as the defendant said, kicking his dog, 3s. ; Jameo Mannion,in Bakehouse Yard, he having been beating his wife on the occasion, ss.—Win. O'Connor, in Mersey-st., ss. DRUNK ON LICENSED PRZEISES.—Bridget Costello was charged with bring drunk on the licensed premises of Frederick Pilling, Royal Oak Inn, Bridge-st. She had had a can by her side when P.S. Longbotham went in, and was speechlessly, drunk, but the landlord said he did not know she wat there.—She was fined ss. PITCH AND Toss.—Charles Parker, 3, Edelsten's-yard, Wm. Shelinerdine, 2, Birchall-st., Thomas Wright, 2, Hardy-st., and Harry Lawton, 22, Lytligoe's-lane, all boys, were fined 2s. 6d. each for playing at pitch and toss for money in Howley-street, on Sunday week. Owen, and E. J. Guest. Demur IN CHARGE OF a Honss.—Henry Taylor, em- ployed by the Corporation, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse, also with cruelty to the animal in Bold-st., the previous morning.—A constable and Inspector Dowty proved the cases. The former stated that the defendant was drunk and whipped the horse unmercifully, and Mr. Dowty said the animal had several wounds upon it.—On the first charge the defen- dant was fined 2s. and on the second ss. and costs. THREATENING.—Joseph Firth, licensed hawker, was charged with threatening William Rogerson, another licensed hawker, his relative, in Flag-lane, on the 15th inst. Mr. Browne defended. A DILINE-DERANGED WANDEZER.—James Alexander Forshaw, married man 16, Manchester-road, was charged with wandering about while in a supposed state of lunacy. Be had been talking about a bottle ot poison he had placed upon the line, and with which he was going to poison himself. His wife stated that he was in the habit of actitig in a strange way when he was drunk. On promising to give up drinking he was discharged. Ass UNLlcriegn Doe.—John Ashbrook, 2, Lilford-d., was charged with keeping a dog without a license, and fined 10s. and costs. Asssum.—" AN Lusa SHlNDT."—Catherine Fallon, 11, Ship-yard, was charged with assaulting Catherine Lee, 20 Ship-yard, on the 15th inst. The complainant said had she known what Warrington was she would never have come into such a place.—Alderman ' Harrison suggested that she should get into a better neighbourhood.—The defendant promised to behave better, but was bound over in £5 to keep the peace for six months, and mulcted in ss. costs.—Owen Mannion, 17 Pitt-st., was charged with assaulting Bridget McGuinness and Thomas her husband, contractor, of Zdward-st., on the 14th inst. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution and Mr. P. Davies for the defence Mr. Browne said the female complainant said she heard a noise in the street about half-past eleven on Saturday night, and on looking out saw Caat her lodger and one of Mannion's lodgers were fighting. Mannion came up and assaulted her severely, and afterwards apologised paying he meant to strike her husband not herself. He also assaulted her husband.—The complainant said the defendant was in his shirt sleeves, and had a poker up one of his sleeves, and knocked them all down on top of her husband."—Other witnesses said they saw bottles flying about, and another said Mannion made a rush for the male complainant and struck his wife.—lr. Davies said there were about 100 persons present at the time, and it was a general shindy—a general Irish row of fists with the men and bottles with the women, Mrs. , McGuinness having one, and having it taken from her. Mannion never struck the complainant. —The , defendant's mother-in-law said there was one bottle thrown, which struck a little girl. Mr. McGuinness pushed some bricks off the wall towards Owen. Mrs. McGuinness prodded her with a bottle, and another witness said Mr. M•Guinness struck Man- nion "because he couldn't hit nobody else." (Laughter.) —The case was withdrawn on an agreement being come to between the solicitors for payment between the parties of the Costs. CRLYELTY TO a FlORSE.—George Baxter, of Woolston, was charged by Inspector Dowry. R.S.P.C.A., with cruelty to a horse by working it While in an unfit state, and Samuel Baxter was charged with causing it to be so worked on the 7th inst. George did not appear. Samuel was fined 20s. and costs, and George was dis- missed.

WARRINGTON V. CREETHAM lllLL.—These ' first-class organisations met for the first time this season a- Arpley, on Saturday. The recollection that the Mant chester club had accounted for Warrington last season- and the fact that Mr. S. M. Crosfield, the popular cap- tain, would figure in the home ranks was sufficient in, ducement for a large crowd to assemble. Despite the heavy downpour of rain on Friday, the wicket was in good condition. Winning the toss, Warrington took up the defence, Messrs. S. M. Crosfield and R. Smith being the first batsmen. The bowling was opened by W. H. Pennington. A single to the captain found Murray oppos- ing him. This bowler was treated lightly, and ten runs all to Crosfield, were the result of his first over. The score steadily rose, and eventually It. Smith overhauled his captain at 37, but this feat had, only been accom- plished when in playing forward at Pennington he was bowled for 18, the highest score of the match. Only a run had been added when Mr. S. M. Crosfield was caught by Coyle, whilst Captain Manson placed one in the hams of short-slip, and Lee failed to survive an appeal for lbw. Thus the third and fourth wickets fell at 41, and the hopes of Warrington sank to a low 'ebb. Clarke had but a short stay, playing on at 45, but some steady batting by J. J. Crosfield and useful hitting by Bell brought on Duck for Coyle at 60. Only six runs had been added when the last corner—Bell—was taken at the wicket. The homesters were not done with yet, and vigorous hitting by Voisey rapidly augmented the score. Duck, to his own astonishment, was no-balled three times in succession, but at 84 had the satisfaction of getting Voisey's wicket with a yorker. Dudar now relieved Pennington, and Crosfield, after' having failed repeatedly with the slows, was stumped, Podmore also falling a victim to Morgan's cleverness L from the next ball. A useful stand was made by •• Dutton and Clark, and the score was taken to 99, 1 when Collier brought off a fine catch in the long field, and the innings closed. The treasurers of some of the big foot3all clubs handle about ao much money as the Chancellors of the Exchequer of sense of the little German States. For instance the sernon's receipts of the Everton Football Club amounted torso les; than £8,624 9s. 7d. Beckon- ing the season at. erne of 36 weeks, it seems that the expenditure amments to nearly £220 on the year's work- ingbot considering the rather disappointing show made by the team, and the unfortunate ground dispute, the financial position is anythitig but embarrassing. Players' wages are 2M38, and travelling expenses £343, while-clothing amounts to £127, sothat the team may be said, to. have cost ire round figures the sum of £6,000'. The Bootle balance sheet is quite modest in comparison', and about £l,OOO will cover the players' 'expenses.

The balance sheet of the Football Association shows a profit orr the year of IWO 6s. 7d., while the actual value of the Association is £3,316 lie. 9d., and as there was a disposable balance of £2,120 10s., it was decided to invest Motber £l,OOO in,Coosols.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

At the Blackburn Rovers Sports, Ames Southworth was again at the post of honour in the sprint races, but although he had to give away sixteen yards start in the 220 yards handicap, he managed by making a desperate effort in the last few yards to win a veryipapular victory right on the tape.

There seems to be a possibility that Morton will during the present season have a further opportunity of "record ' breaking" with some of the Southern cracks as competi- tors. Heath's recent performances stamp him as the coming champion for distances of one or two miles, whilst there does not seem to exist any reason why he should not be equally good up to ten miles: A five miles race with Morton, Heath, Kibblewhite, and Parry in their best form, or one of ten miles with Thomas included,, would be sure to attract an Immense attendance, especial- ly if the proceeds were devoted to some charitable object, which admirable suggestion has, we understandAemana- ted from Morton himself.

The final tie for the 200• Guinea Challenge Shield, under theauspices of the National Physical) Recreation Society, was decided in the Kinnaird Hall, .Dundee, on Saturday evening. The hall, seated for between two and three thousand people, was crowded. The teams which had so face one another were those of Exeter Hall, Gymnasium, London,. and Aberdeen Gymnastic and Rowing Club. The judges were Sergeant-Major Nokes, ' Chief Instructor to the .British Army, Aldershot • and Mr. J. M. Hubbard,director of the Birmingham" Athletic Institute, while Mr. Chesterton, director of physical exercises for the London School Board, was referee. The London men won on the jumping two points, but lost on the Indian clubs by nine points, and ou the rings by eight points. The grand total of the Aberdeen men was 375, leaving them the winners of the Shield by 15 points., The decision of the judges gave complete satis- 'faction, none of them being called in question by the competitors or andience. The jumping competition created the greatest amount of interest, the rivalry in the last two taking place between Lane for the London team and Williams for the Aberdeen team. Lane is of great fame in jumping,, having won the first prize for it at both the Orion and German Gymnasium Clubs, London, open competition. Nye, of London, cleared only sft. 4in., though greater things were expected of him. For this he got 151 marks only. Lane was now left in the London team against Dugan and Williams for Aberdeen, the former of whom went out in attempting sft. Bin,, which was cleared by Lane and Williams. Both of these cleared sft. 7in., and both failed to clear 5f t. Bin.

div.head: CONVICT DEEMING.
div.p: THE CONVICT DEEMING.

It is stated that Deeming las made a will, bequeath- ing his effects and the biography which he has been writing since his imprisonment to Mr. Lyle, his solicitor, who is also appointed executor. The prisoner directs that one-tenth of the proceeds arising from the publica- tion of the biography and the sale of his effects is to be given to Miss Rounsevell. It is understood that if Deeming's head be handed to the doctors for examination after the execution, it will, at the condemned man's own request, be given to three doctors who were not connected with the trial. heY will examine and photograph the brain, which will after- wards be frozen and sent to the European medical schools for critical analysis. The Board appointed to adjudicate on the twenty claims sent in for the reward of £lOO offered by the Victorian Government fcr the apprehension of the Windsor murderer have decided to divide the amount amongst seventeen of the witnesses who gave evidence at the recent trial.

div.head: PETITION TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL,
div.p: PETITION TO THE PRIVY COUNCIL,

The Governor ofrVictoria has declined to accede to the petition for the postponement for a week of the date of Deeming's execution. The petition to the Privy Council. prepared by a firm of London solicitors at the request of Deeming's Mel- bourne solicitor,, was lodged on Wednesday morning, and, it has been arranged, will be heard to-day. The petition urges that the verdict of the Jury was against the weight of evidence : that the convict was at the time of the Melbourne murder, and is now, insane; that he was not granted a fair trial, and that insufficient time was allowed for preparation of his defence. The peti- tion is also largely founded upon and accompanied by declarations made by the convict's brother, Edward Deeming and the wife of Edward Deeming, as to the eceentncitiesand insanity of the convict from his youth up. The declarations have also been sent to Melbourne. The texts of Edward Deerning's declaration and of the petition were lodged on Wednesday with the Privy Council

div.head: PETITION REFUSED.
div.p: THE PETITION REFUSED.

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council met on Thursday, to consider the petition presented on behalf of the convict Deeming, praying for a respite. The noble and learned lords' present were the Lord Chancellor, Lords Watson, Herschell, MacNaghten, Morris, Hannen, and Shand, and Sir R. Couch. The court was crowded, some ladies being present. Mr. Geoghegan, who, with Mr. Lawless, appeared for the petitioner, briefly re- corded the circumstances under which he came before committee. He said he asked for a respite in order that documents on their way from Australia might be pro-' duced. The Lord Chancellor ohserved that they were on a point of law, and had no affidavits before them. Mr. Geoghegan said the sOtutory declarations on their way to Australia made by Deeming's brother and sister-in- law strongly corroborated the theory that the convict was of unsound mind. After haring counsel's argu- ments, the Lord Chancellor said he did not think they could entertain any argument on the question of the convict's sanity. On the question of law, it had been laid down as the invariable practice that legal decisions in the Colonies should not be interfered with* except in cases of grave injustice. The committee would humbly advise her Majesty that this was not a ease for the Crown's interference.
