div.head: LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARY.
div.p: LANCASHIRE GOOD TEMPLARY.

The No. 1 Convention, South-West Lancashire district, held its quarterly meeting in the Wesleyan Mission-room, Buttermarket-street, on Saturday, when, in addition to representatives from the five lodges of the town, a good number were present from Earlestown, Hindley, Manchester, St. Helens, Widnes, and Wigan. Bro. Colour-Sergeant Mantle (Warrington), C.C. Templar, presided, being sup- ported by nearly the whole of the Convention officers The officer's report showed that the itdult membership of the whole ordef in England was 55,70; the juvenile branoh. 52,427 ; of which we had in South- West Lancashire 2,331 adults, and 1,903 juveniles; the membership of the Convention being, according to latest reports, 406 adults in 15 lodges. A new lodge had been recently opened at Thatto Heath (St. Helens) under fav- ourable circumstances. The Treasurer reported a balance in hand, with some assets and no liabilities. The juvenile competitive examination was, after some. discussion, postponed to the winter session. The death of Bro. H. Yeatman, a representative from St. Helens, having been reported, Bro. Clarke (Earlastown) moved, and Bro. Linden (St. Helens) seconded, a vote of condo- lence and sympathy to the widow. This was carried by a standing vote. On the question of separation from South-West Lancashire district and the conversion, of the convention into a district lodge, to be Wield the South Lancashire district, a long discussion ensued, it being eventually decided by a three-fourth majority of, the representatives to agitate for the change. The lodges at Peasley Cross and Widnes being reported weak, arrangements were made for spEcial meetings to revive them. It was decided to hold the next session at Widnes. Thanks having been voted too the Walter none- hill" Lodge, VVarritigton, for the excellent arrange- ments for the gathering, the Session was closed at 7 p.m., after which tea was ,partaken of. A short open-air meeting followed, and a public meeting was opened soon after 8 p.m., Bro. Mantle presiding, being supported by Bros. Quartermaster-Sergeant Roberts, (Warrington), Breckbank (St. Helens), Clarke (Earles- town), and Scaife (St. Helens). After a short address by the Chairman, the following entertainment was ren- dered—Sister Lucy Sheath (recitation), Bro. Skaife (address), Sister We. Sheath (song), Sister Mortimore (recitation), Bro. Rogerson (song), Bro. Sheath (recita- tion), Bro. Rwberts (address), Bro. Newns (song), Bro. Chadwick (recitation), Sister Sheath (song), Sister Wii, lett (recitation), Bro. Rogerson (song), Sister Crocker (recitation), Bro. Rogerson (song). A vote of thanksto the Chairman and also to the members who entertained followed, and the meeting was closed with the National. Anthem at 10 p.ra.

But wot upset Owd Bill so mitch, Wuz wot hoo'd hey to eyt Hoo wudn't look at wot wun thowt The best o' powltry meyt., Hoo hated curn, but rayther liked Lung hob nails an' tin tacks, ' Wi' just a tit, o'th' flavourie 0' Web& eends an'iwas r Ez yo may readily suppose, Hoo neaw an' then took ill, Wicti browt thoose rinkles on the broo 0' poor owd Birlcy Bill! To put her reet, he geet a knife An' cut th' owd iron eawt ; An' wen he'd stitched her up agen, Hoo clock'd, an' hopp'd abeawt ! But, woss then that, boo took the "pip," An' bed a shockin' cough; So just to get her trubbles o'er, He chopp'd her yed clean oft! Yo're wrung if yo itnagine that This physic didn't fail; .Fer th' yed kept oppenin'' an' gaped, Wile th' body wriggle'dth' tail!! By Gyow ! this war a corker, lads! An' owd Bill thowt so too;. Thus eends my tale—aw think its true— But thoose may deaubt ez will; No gradely judge ull-ever deaubt The word o' Bliley Bill! Nyowton, God bless 0','20, 5, 1892.

REFORM IN TIIE PATENT LAW.

Sir,—Since writing you on the 13th ulto., R 7 e have had many instances brought before our notice, and many letters from patentees, showing that patents are allowed to lapse at the end of the 4th and sth years be- cause the patentee has not been remunerated in that length of time for the time and expense incurred in bringing his invention on to the market, and is unable or unwil'ing to pay the heavy fees demanded for main- taining the patent in force. Some people think that the lapsing of such patents is a benefit to trade rather than the reverse, but after a long experience of patents and patentees our opinion is decidedly that it is not so, as the patentee looses all incentive to push the matter further and no one else will then spend anything on it to complete or perfect it, knowing that as soon as they have succeeded others can at once copy and compete with them.

It has been well said that if " Necessity is the mother of inveLticn, the patent law is the father of inventi on," but our cr-^ent law is so unpaternat that it seeks to, and succeee.s I, choking off its own offspring at the age of four or trs J years, when they have just begun to stand alone, ,oft:l_ the exception of such precocious ones as are able to scamper out of reach. We should be pleased to see the renewal fees abolished altogether, but such is too much to expect at once, but a small fee such as we proposed, commencing at Ll. would not Nit felt much of a burden,would be sufficiently high to kill useless patents without hurting sych as would afterwards prove valuable, and would not to a serious extent affect the revenue,—Yours truly,_
WM. P. THOMPSON AND "do. Patent Agents. 6, Bank-st., Manchester, 16th May 1892.

POLITICAL PARTIES AND WORKING-MEN. Sir,—Too little attention, has. I fear, ;been paid by the working-men of Warrington to the letters addressed to your neutral contemporary by Mr. J. S. Leadam, the Liberal candidate for the Altrincham division, one of which appeared on the 26th of March, and the other on the 14th of May. They are in answer to the letters of a correspondent of a " local contemporary," signing himself " A Tory Working-man," and contain a com- plete refutation, based on authentic records, to which Mr. Leadam specially refers, of the assertions made by this Tory, that to the Tories, and not to the Liberals, is to be attributed the legislation which, so far as it has yet gone, forms the charter of the rights and liberties of the working-classes. From the admirable speeches delivered by Mr. Leadam in Warrington, last month, his great knowledge of the true history of legislation be- came clearly apparent to his hearers, and in these two letters there is more valuable information on the sub- ject of the extent to which working-men are indebted to each of the rival parties, than I ever saw expressed within the same limits. This nec.ssary condensation renders them, perhaps, somewhat less attractive to casual readers, than they would otherwise be; but they deserve tee careful perusal and study of everyone who desires to form a sound opinion on this very important subject. Mr. Leadam takes his readers back to the beginning of the century, when Sir Robert Peel, the father of the great minister, succeeded, much to his credit, in getting passed a bill, known as " 'rhe Health and Morals Act, which, in the case of apprentices in cotton and woollen mills, prohibited night work, and limited their-hours of work by day to twelve, but which was from the first unworkable, because its enforcement was entrusted to the magistrates, who were all employers themselves. From this point Mr. Leadam traces the history of such legislation, and shows how the efforts of men like the great Liberal lawyer. Sir Samuel Romilly, the distin- guished socialist, Richard Owen, the eminent Whig, Francis Horner, the earnest philanthropist, Lord Ash- ley, afterward Lord Shaftesbury,the prominent Radicals Sir F. Bennett and Sir John Cam Hobhouse, and a series of others, including Lord Morpeth, and Lord Al- thorp, were opposed and frustrated by the Tory leaders, and the Tory party, backed up by the Rouse of Lords, while they had the sympathy and support of the Liberal leaders, including Lord Melbourne and Lord Palmerston, and their followers. This fact is well illustrated by the efforts made by Lord Ashley in 1844 and 1846 to restrict the working hours of young persons to ten. They were supported by Lord John Russell, the head of the Liberal party, Sir George Grey, Home Secretary in his adminis- tration, Mr. (afterwards Lord) Macaulay, and other leading Liberals, whereas they were bitterly and success- fully opposed by Sir Robert Peel and the whole strength of the Tory party, as "Jack Cade legislation," until 1647, when Lord John Russell's administration had come into power, and the bill was carried. •Quite as effectually does Mr. Leadem dispose of the other claims of the Tories to be the real friends of the working-man. The hardihood with which they take credit for such measures as the Employers' Liability Act, which was passed by Mr. Gladstone, in 1880, in the teeth of their opposition, is only to be accounted for by the fact that they consider that working-men are stupid and ignorant enough to believe anything they are told ; while their cool effrontery in asserting that working-men owe to the Tories the legalisation of Trades Unions, because they passed in 1875 an act relating to trade disputes, assumes that the memory of a working-man is not exten- tive enough to carry him back to 1889, when Mr. Glad- stone passed his hill for protecting the funds of Trades' Unions, or to 1871, when he carried the great measure by which those bodies were placed upon a recognised and unassailable basis.

div.head: CONSERVATIVES AND TIIE WORKINGMEN.
div.p: THE CONSERVATIVES AND TIIE WORKING- MEN.

Sir,—l see that a correspondent of your local Tory contemporary claims that certain statements have corn- pletely smashed the huge fiction that the Conserva- tives have never done anything for the working-man." Well, I should imagine that what fictiop pertains to this matter lies in the supposition that intelligent and
- impartial Liberals would assert that the Conserva-

,tives had done absolutely nothing for the working-man. They certainly have passed some good and needful . measures in the interests of that class, or there could not possibly exist among some benighted working-men
the gross delusion by which they arc so infatuated: that

• their most ardent friends are the Conservatives. The • Tory party have found 4t absolutely necessary to do something for the work Mg-classes, just as the American , slavek,viners found it necessary to do something for their slaves, the object being in the one case as in the other to
conciliate public opinioavpzudence,and contentment with -

hateful system of servitucl, so that that detestable :system might be the better maintained. .The argument .by the Camservatives that because they have done a certain amount of good to the working-men, therefore their ascendancy should be perpetuated is like that of ,she American slaver that because he transferred certain material benefits on his slave, therefore the institution of-slavery shculd be preserved.

The Conservatives have the audacity to boast cf the measures they,have passed for the benefit of the work- ingecan. Since 1867, for instance, and they have the audacity to claim also, that the bill of enfranchisement which was passed in that year was conferred upon the workinginen by a Tory Government. The Tories were in power it is true, when the Bill was passed, but., as Lord Salisbury himself admitted, it was due entirely to the amendments of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Bright, and other Liberal members and the determined stand they made against the monstrous provisions it contained when brought in by Mr. Disraeli, and which would have made the condition of the working-classes worse titan before,that ' it was passed in its present form, and thus becabue blessing instead of a curse to the working-classes. The Conservatives have the astollnding impudence to make this Act one of the grounds of appeal to the constitu, ents to support Lord Salis'oury-, when he himself resigned his seat in the Tory cabinet, as did two other mernhers of it, rather than sopport the measure, And we have his own authority ;for spying that he lla.s /19

claim to support on any such around. The Conserva- tives obstinately opposed the Bill, well knowing what vast consequences it would involve, and the concessions it would force them to make to the working classes, and they now claim credit for these concessions just as if they had made them voluntatily, and they were essen- tial and .natural and not forced products of Conserva- tism. Every one of these measures they in effect effaced ley opposing the Reform Bill of 1867 as altered by the Liberals. And can any impartial politician be- tieve that had it not been for that measure and the Bal- lot Bill previously passed by a Liberal Government, in the face of the fiercest antagonism from the I Conserva- tives, the measures for which they are now so loudly demanding credit from the working classes would ever have been passed. The correspondent of your Tory con- temporary claims with characteristic Tory effrontery that factory legislation was due to the Conservatives. He does so, I suppose on the ground, though he does not say so, that the Conservatives passed Factory Acts in the years' 1844, 1845, 1867, 1874 and 1878. But the two last-named Bills only carried out principles laid down in others previously introduced by Liberals, and the Act of 1878 was merely a consolidation of fifteen previous Acts, all of which, except the four I have just cited, were passed by Liberal Governments. The Conservative correspondent also claims that it is the Tories who are to be thanked for trades union legisla- tion. But it was the Liberal pa.xty that legalised trades unions and estabtished them on a secure basis so far as the protection of their funds were concerned, namely, 'by the Act passed in 1871. Free education is credited to the present Parliament, by the same untrutlthil Con- servative champion, though, as a matter of fact, a majority of the Conservatives in the House of Commons voted against it and it was really carried by the Liberal vote.

. _ To deal in this letter, categorically, with the c(ndless and almost innumerable misstatements which the Con- servatives are at present making in Warrington by their local newspaper, by placards, and by pamphlets, would necessitate considerably more space than .you will be disposed to allow me in the number of your paper in ' which, with your permission, this communication will appear. The Conservatives are circulating lies broad- cast, on the principle, I suppose, of allowing for the highest possible discount that may be put upon their assertions. They are trying to deceive the working- men electors in the most egregious fashion by claim- ing in print that the Conservatives have passed more measures for the benefit of the working- man than the Tories have during certain periods; and they do this by taking credit for all measures passed during times of Conservative administration by Liberal votes, and-by excluding from consideration about half the measures passed by the Liberals. But the readiest way to determine the question of which party has passed the largest number of, and the most important measures for the welfare of the masses, would be for a Conservative and myself to take two equal periods of Tory and of Liberal government, and let us each adduce all the measures that we can bring forward on our indi- vidual sides for that period ; and then leave our readers to decide accordingly.—Yours truly, .
-.- . MANLIUS. • [We shall be quite willing to open out columns to any Conservative who thinks he can make out a case.— En. E.r.l
4' A RENVOLE SOMEWHERE !"

ANOTHER TORY WAIL. No wonder that I'm feeling ill, And need a powerful draught or White lies are sticking in my gill— There's a Rent-'ole somewhere! " Whene'er I take my walks" around, I hear this melancholy sound, "Lord, Lord 1 how fast we're losing ground,"— There's a Rent-'ole somewhere ! Our Canvassers are in the dumps, They go about their work like chumps, And won't—or cannot—stir their stumps— There's a Rentiole somewhere ! Our Chaifan looks dismayed—amazed,— Abashed, cadaverous, and dazed, And almost absolutely crazed— There's a Rent'-ole somewhere! Our candidate looks" blue "as well, Not " merry as a marriage bell," But hopeless,—if he'd only tell- -. . . .
There's a Ren't'-ole somewhere ! Our Poet tries his hand in vain, But fails in the triumphant strain, Save when he's cribbing, might and
There's a Rent-'ole somewhere 1

Yes ! cribs I—and never owns the source, Whence he describes, Aith fire and force, Our down-grade ignominious course— There's a Reut-'ole somewhere ! No wonder that we feel morose, When reading such a hashed-up dose— All worthy of the Poet Close— There's a Rent-'ole somewhere!

I buy -air paper twice—a week, And its consummate wash ' and 'cheek,' Makes me inclined to " eat the leek " There's a Rent-'ole somewhere! If what's a-doing, I would know, In grumbling tones I'm told to go Te Ilades—or to—well,—'Below ! _ .

There's a Rent-'ole somewhere! It's plain to see, we're in a "frost," And we can safely count the cost— Which means, Great Scott! our Cause is lost ! There's a Rent-'ole somewhere ! Soon we'll be Tories unattached— Our candidate is overmatched, And might as well be drawn or' scratched ! There's a Rent-'ole somewhere! FUNNYDOSS. Warrington, May 19th, 1892.
DEATH OF MR. E. GREENALL OF GRA PPENHALL.

The death took place on Tuesday afternoon of Mr. Edward Greenall, J.P., of Grappenhall Hall. Mr. Greenall, who was 71 years of age, had been in fail- ing health for a considerable time past, and, as we have before mentioned, his condition had been hopeless for the last week or two. He was the eldest son of the late Mr. .Thomas Greenall of Grap- penhall Hall, who died in 1847, and was born at Wilderspool in 1820. In 1847 he married Anne, daughter of the late Mr. Peter Greenall, who was at one time member for Wigan and who died at St. Helens in 1845. The deceased gentleman was one of the oldest local magistrates for the West Derby Hundred having been placed on the Commission of the Peace so far back as the 25th August, 1858. He was also a magistrate for the County of Cheshire; and, being a senior justice, always presided when he was able to be present at the Daresbary Petty Sessions. He was also occasionally to be seen on the Bench at the Warring- ton Petty Sessions. For over 20 years he was chairman of the Daresbury Highway Board, the meetings of which he rarely failed to attend, and on his resignation a com- paratively short time ago, he was succeeded by Mr. J. Charlton Parr. Mr. Greenall was one of the directors of Parr's Banking Company, Limited, having been a partner in the Bank previoes to its being turned into a Limited Company. Mr. Greenall was also connected with the Weaver Trust, and was for some years a member of the Cheshire County Police and Licensing Committee under the old administration. Though he took no active part in political matters, he was a warm supporter of the Conservative cause. He was a member ot the Church of England, and attended the services held at the Parish Cure{ at Grappenhall, of which Iris brother, the Rev. Canon Greenall, is rector. He has let a widow and five sons and a daughter to mourn hic loss—Mr. Edward Greenall, who is Mayor of Warrington • Mr. Peter Greenall, of London.; Mr. Henry Greenall, E,alicitor, Warrington; Mr. Alfred Greenall and Mr. Frank ‘Greenall, and Mrs. W. C. Jones, of "The Oaklands." . . .

------- It may be 'mentioned that the death took place on the very day that had been fixed for an "At Home" by the Mayer, a son of the deceased. The gathering had, how- ever, been previiously postponed. The interment takes place to-day in Grappenhall churchyard. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES.

At the Warrington County Sessions on Wednesday, Mr. John Rylands who occupied the chair at the open- ing of the court, referred to the death of Mr. Greenall He remarked that not only was the deceased' gentleman well respected but he deserved to be. He had seen him .en that bench under trying circumstances, and had never once had any ground for differing from anything he had said.— Mr. W. H. Bleckly who was also on the Bench said he endorsed the remaz ks that had fallen from Mr. Rylands. They had sustained a very great loss.—Major Pickmere said Mr. Greenall was liked by not only the county, but also the borough, magistrates, and, he was sure, by the town generally for his urbanity and kindness to all.

WIDNES POLICE COURT,
MONDAY.—Before Messrs. -S,;Preten- -Bie-tlierton and J. Lister. _ _ .

DnuNkENNEss.—Mary Ann Corbett, Nelson-st. ; John Cooney, Peel-st. ; Thos. Rourke, Alfred-st. ; Dominick Dovitch, Water-st. THEFT FROM A WASTE HEAP.—Susan Quinn (18) Pleasant-st. ; Patrick Daley (13), Moss-st. ; and John Boyle (17), Moss-st., were charged with stealing a quan- tity of iron bolts, the property of the United Alkali Company, from a waste tip near Moor-lane.—Bernard Matheson, Rose Terrace, Ditton, foreman labourer on the waste tip,said be saw the two boys on Thursday afternoon picking the bolts up, and throwing them to the female defendant. div.head: WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.
div.p: WOMEN'S LIBERAL FEDERATION.

The annual Council meetings of the Women's Liberal Federation began on Thursday, in London. Lady Aberdeen presided, and said Mrs. Gladstone had asked her to give a welcome to the delegates in her name. They had gathered, she said, to do high and responsible work on the eve of a national cri,ds, but if they were imbued with the spirit of true Liberalism all would be well. The adoption of the report was moved by th. r

seconding the motion Lady Carlisle referred to the question of women's suffrage, and advocated unity. Other speakers urged that nothing should be done to jeopardise Home Rule. It was explained that Mrs.Oladstone and Lady Aberdeen had no intention of resigning their positions on the Federation, and the report was adopted. A resolution was carried in favour of the provision of lady speakers to visit the affiliated associations. The amendment of which notice had been given relating toParliamen- tary enfranchisement was withdrawn, and Lady Carlisle moved a resolution to the effect that the Council should instruct the Executive Committee to promote the enfranchisrnent of women (including the local and Parliamentary votes for all women— married, single, or widowed—who possessed any of the legal qualifications entitling men to vote)among the other Liberal reforms now before the country, while not:making it a test question at the general election. After several ladies, inzluding Mrs. Jacob Bright, had spoken,the resolution was carried,with twelve disz-entients.

On Wednesday the session was resumed under the presidency of Lady Aberdeen. Interesting discus- sions took place on Home Rule, the economic posi- tion of women, the shop hours question, the divorpe law, disestablishment, and the liquor traffic.—Lord Henry Somerset moved a resolution in favour of local option.—Miss Bessie Dutton (Warrington), who seconded the motion, said that this was pre- eminently a woman's question.—At a public meet- ing in the evening Lady Aberdeen—the wife of a former Viceroy of Ireland—took up the question of "Ulster," and showed that it was only one corner of that province to which Lord Salisbury could appeal, and she very much doubted whether the practical Ulstermen would respond to his recent suggestions. Addresses were delivered by Mr. Stansfeld, M.P., Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., and others ; and resolutions heartily supporting the Liberal leaders were passed with acclamation.

On Thursday an open Conference in connection with the Women's Liberal Federation was held in London. Lady Aberdeen presided. It was resolved that a measure of Poor-law reform was urgently needea, coupled with better administration; that the property qualification for Poor-law Guardians should be abolished; that the mode of voting be by ballot; and that women should be members of every board of guardians. A resolution was also carried in favour of further legislation for the pro- tection of children, with special reference to the question of infant insurance. The Conference urged that disputes between nations should be settled by arbitration instead of by war, and discussed the evils of the opium traffic and the injustice .of min- ing royalties. The deputation to the Federation meeting from Warrington consisted of Mrs. Houston, Mrs. •Winser. Mrs. R. Garnett, and Miss B. Dutton.

div.head: CHEMICAL AND COPPER FUMES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: CHEMICAL AND COPPER FUMES AT ST. HELENS.

The Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority hate been in communication with the Local Government Board regarding the emission of noxious fumes from the chemical and copper works at St. Ifelens. The Clerk to the Authority forwarded to the Board a copy of a communication on the subject received from certain inhabitants of their district, and en- closed some thorn cuttings showing the disastrous effects on vegetation. At the last meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority a letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that the thorn cuttings had been examined by Mr. Fletcher, the chief inspector under the Alkali Acts, and it appeared from his examination that the noxious agents which had principally injured fhe thorns were sulphurous and sulphuric acids. Mr. Fletcher had informed the Board that those acids were discharged from copper works and from works iu which Chance's process for the recovery of salphur from alkali waste was carded on, but that in the Widnes Rural Sanitary District they were also discharged in very largo quantities from all chemical and ether: works as ingredients of common coal smoke, owing to the sulphurous nature of the coal used. The Board explained that as neither copper atmelting pro- cesses, nor Chance's process for the recovery .of sulphur, nor the emission of smoke from manufacttries came within the purview of the Alkali Acts they were riot em- powered to take any action as to alleged nuisances from those sources, under section 27 of the Alkali Act. The Chairman (Mr. T. Kenwright) remarked that he had noticed Mr. Ritchie had introduced in the House of Conmons a Bill to amend the A;kalia Act of 1881, awl the process for the recovery of AulphOr from 4-1J5.21.i waste was scheduled.

div.head: WARRINGTON C A.NDIDATE S. QUESTIONS BY RAILWAY SERVANTS.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON C A.NDIDATE S. QUESTIONS BY RAILWAY SERVANTS.

The Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, of which Mr. Edward Harford is the General Secre- tary, are putting questions, through their various branches, to candidates for Parliamentary honours. We had occasion the other week to publish the answers received from the candidates for the North- wick Division and the Runcorn Division, and to comment on the unfavourable character of the re- plies of the Tory candidates as compared with those given by the Liberal candidates. From the letters printed below, it will be seen that the same holds good as to Warrington, for while Dr. Houston deals with each question separately, Mr. Robert Pierpoint has sent an answer which is no answer at all. It is true it purports to be a preliminary reply, but this preliminary reply was de3patched on the 3rd May. No other reply being forthcoming, the local secre- tary has made the correspondence public, as was ' intimated would be done when the questions were ' originally submitted. The communications sent to both candidates were as follows: _

QUESTIONS.—" 1. A maximum working day of ten hours, with six days to the week, for all rail- way employes, such hours to be regulated and en- forced by the Board of Trade, the necessary powers being obtained for that purpose from Parliament. 2. An effective supervision over the working of all rail- ways, which shall include periodical inspection by qualified and practical sub-inspectors, who shall act under the existing Board of Trade inspectors. 3. Board of Trade inquiries to be held in all cases of serious accidents to employes where such occur in tho movement of vehicles, and not, as now, to be mainly confined to accidents in which the public safety is directly involved. 4. Railway Companies to I be compelled to provide self-acting coupling appliances ' for shunters and effective protection for platelayers when working on the permanent way during the course of public traffic, and that wherever possible automatic fog signalling be substituted for the present system. 5. Certificates of competency, on the lines laid down in the measure commonly known as the En&rinemen's Certifi- cate Bill, to be held by all engine drivers, without which it shall be illegal for anyone to take charge of an engine. The Board of Trade to grant the certificates, which shall be altogether independent of the companies. 6. An Employers' Liability Act, on the lines of the Bill introduced by Mr. T. Burt, M.P., in which the un- just doctrine of common employment shall have no place, and contracting out be made illegal. The amount which may be claimed shall he unlimited, as in ordinary common law, while the period for giving notice of in- tention to procsed under the Act shall be extended to six months. 7. Payment of all members of Parliament and of official election expenses by the State. In order to put all candidates on an equal footing, the payments must be general, and not confined to labour members."
MR. ROBERT PIERPOINT'S REPLY. St. Austin's, Warrington May 3rd, 1862.

Dear Sir, I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of April 30th, enclosing a paper containing certain ques- tions. They are not matters to be treated off-hand, but they shall have my attention. In writing these few preliminary lines, I think that I need scarcely assure you of the interest that I take in men employed on the railways. I am, dear sir, yours faithfully, ROBERT PIERPOIN r.

div.head: DR. HOUSTON'S IMPLY. 52 Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin, May sth, 1892.
div.p: DR. HOUSTON'S IMPLY. 52 Fitzwilliam Square, Dublin, May sth, 1892.
Dear Sir,—

In reply to your letter of the 30th ult., which has been forwarded to me from Warrington, I beg to append specific answers to the several questions therein referred to. I wish to add, by way of explanation,that while the Board of Trade may be, and probably is, the body most suitable for the discharge of the duties contemplated by questions numbered 1,3, and 5, I think it is desirable that a candidate should hold himself free to form an opinion on that subject, in case some alteration should be proposed. 1. lam in favour of a maximum working day of 10 hours, with six days to the week, for all railway em- Ployes, this limit to be enforced by statute : the method by wttich its regulation and enforcement are to be effected I prefer to leave an open question. 2. lam in favour of effective supervision over rail- ways, and in the manner proposed. 3. lam in favour of the holding of proper public inquiries in the cases contemplated by this question : but prefer not to bind myself to more details. 4 lam in favour of all these things, so far as they are capable of being carried out: but,while I understand that self-acting coupling appliances are in all cases practicable, I am not sufficiently conversant with the working of railways to be able to form an opinion whether effective protection for platelayers, when work- ing on the permanent way, during the course of public traffic, can be provided. 5. lam in favour of certificates of competency being required from all engine-drivers, and I am in favour of vesting the power of granting such certificates in some body entirely independent of the Railway Companies: but I prefer to leave the question of the constitution of that body an open one. 6. lam in favour of such an Act. 7. lam in favour of payment of members of Parlia- ment and of official election expenses out of public monies. All members, whether labour representatives or not, should in my opinion be entitled to receive pay- ment.—Yours faithfully, ARTHUR HOUSTON.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. W. WALLINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. W. WALLINGTON.

It is with much regret that we record the death of Mr. Wm. Wallington, an old and respected W ar- ringtonian. Mr. Wallington had been ailing, more or less, for two or three years back, suffering from a complaint of the heart,and on Monday morning he died at his residence in St. Ma's-st., Latchford. Deceased, though not born in Warrington, came to this town along with the rest of his family from Stockport when quite young, and had lived in Warrington ever since. By trade he was a white- smith and engineer, and carried on business near Warrington bridge. For thirty or more years he was closely connected with the Congregational denomination, and, being an earnest worker, he has held many offices in connection with Wycliffe Church and Sunday School, and at the time of the death he was one of the deacons of the church. In other respects he did not take any prominent part in public work. He lived an unostentatious life, and was highly respected by all who knew him. He was 68 years of age, and leaves a widow but no children. It may be mentioned that all of the five brothers, of whom de- ceased was one have died within a period of four or five years, four of them dying within a space of about two years. Tke first on the death-roll was Mr. John Wall- ington, who lived at Northwich ; then followed in quick succession Mr. George Wallington, builder, War- rington; Mr. T. Wallington of Latchford: and Mr. Elisha Wallington, who lived in Bewsey-road, and the last of the five is the gentleman whose death we have recorded above. .

_ The funeral took place at Hill Cliffe, on Thursday afternoon. The Rev. John Davies conducted a short service at the residence of the deceased, and the ser- vice at Hill Chile was conducted by the Rey. Mr. Kea- worthy. After the service at Hill Chffe the coffin was borne to the gravt by the following nephews of the de- ceased:—Mr. H. Wallington, Mr. G. Wallington. Mr. E. Wallington, Mr. W. H. Wallington, Mr. T. Wallington, and Mr.Wallington(Grappenhall). The coffin was followed by the following relatives and friends :—Mr. Atkinson and Mr. Forster, brothers-in-law; Messrs. W. Ford, J. W. Bouchier, and Messrs. Z. Armitage, A. H. Lee, J. S. Garland, J. Padmoro, R. Wylie, W. Beswick, and T. Hawthorne, deacons of Wycliffe Church; Messrs. Haynes, J. Westgarth, J. Renworthy, W. Roberts, Pick- avance, and England,members of Wycliffe congregation. At the grave side there was a numerous gathering of ladies of the Church and congregation. The coffin which was covered with beautiful wreaths, bore the following inscription :--" William Wallington, died May 18th, 1892, aged 68 years."

div.head: SUBSIDENCE AT NORTHWICII.
div.p: SUBSIDENCE AT NORTHWICII.

A serious subsidence occurred at Northwich early on Thursday morning when a large block of buildings in Castle-st., occupied by Mr. Dixon, solicitor, collapsed with a terrible crash, the noise of which was heard throughout the town. The foundations entirely dis- appeared. the building toppled over, and a considerable portion of it fell into the chasm. The premises are practically destroyed, and the contents were with much difficulty removed.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF SHALLPDX AT
div.p: OUTBREAK OF SHALLPDX AT

WARRINGTON. There are at present, we are sorry to say, three persons in the Warrington hospital suffering from smallpox. The family in which the outbreak took place came from near Halifax, Yorkshire, but removed to Warrington at the beginning of this month, and took a house in Latchford, just outside the borough boundary. Some of them were taken ill, and on a doctor being called in it was found that they were suffering from smallpox. This was ascertained on the 10th, but owing to there being no provisions for compulsory notification in the rural district as there is in the borough, the cases were not reported to the authorities, and therefore, the immediate isolation which is so very desirable in cases of this kind was not secured. The circum- stances having, however, come to the ears of Dr. Fox, who was acting for the time being as the de- puty of Dr. Gornall, the •Medical Officer of Health, steps were taken on the 15th to have the three patients removed to the hospital. The smallpox is of a pronounced type, but not of a severe nature. The patients are at present doing well, and there has not yet been any further outbreak. The subject of this outbreak was, we understand, considered by the Sanitary Committee at a meeting on Wednesday evening, and the Committee passed a resolution urging the Rural Sanitary Authority to adopt at an early date the compulsory Notification Act, and there was a hope expressed that the Rural Sanitary Authority would make terms with the Corporation relative to the admission of their ' patients to the Corporation hospital. It need hardly be pointed out that there is much to be said in favour of such a course, this latest case in itself being a strong argument in support of both com- pulsory notification and of the necessity of having the means of immediate isolation. The Warrington Corporation nave powers to extend their hospital, and probably they would proceed to utilise those powers if an agreement were entered into with the ,rural authorities. Since the above was written we understand that Dr. Gornall, the Medical Officer of Health, has ascertained that a person suffering from smallpox has been living in the same yard as the other patients unknown to the authwities.
SCARLET FEVER AT WARRINGTON.

There has lately been a considerable increase in the number ,of scarlet fever cases in the borough and in the rural districts adjoining, and there are now between forty and fifty cases in the Fever Hospital.

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of this Club was held at the Workmen's Club, Market Place, on Thursday even- ing. There was a large attendance. Mr. T. Din- widdie presided at the commencement of the meet- ing, and afterwards Councillor Tinsley and Mr. Percy Davies, who had been elected president.

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: THE SECRETARY'S REPORT.

The Hon. Secretary, (Mr. J. E. Warren), in his report, with regard to the first team, says : " I am pleased again to be in a position to report a most successful season for cur club. Every time I come to write my annual report I feel more pride in the club with which I have been so long and so intimately con- nected. True to our motto (Excelsior) we climb higher year by year up the ladder of fame, until we are becom- ing the envy of Lancashire clubs. The bickerings and cliqueism which was so prominent a feature in the his- tory of the club some years ago seemed to have died a natural death. The way in which the officers perform their duties, the success of the players in their matches, and the entire harmony which prevails in the club, from the president down to the humblest official, leave very little standing ground for carping critics. Since I was reappointed your secretary in 1886, I have laid myself out to gradually, but thoroughly organise and place under competent control the various departments of reporting, field, team, sports management, the clothing department, &c., &c., and so well supported have I been by the various Committees that I have had to work with, that I think the members may now congratulate themselves on belonging to one of the best organised clubs in England." As you are aware the writer had the honour of being elected a member of the Lancashire County Committee last year and has attended every meeting since. We must congratulate ourselves on the distinction attained by our players James Jolley and James T. Bate. Jolley was elected to play forward for Lancashire against Cheshire, and Bate has played in four matches, been selected to play in two others which were abandoned, and has been reserve half-back for every other Lanca- shire match ads aoz3on. Although lie did not play against Yorkshire which is one of the conditions to qualify, the Committee have decided to give Bate his cap. The annual sports were fairly successful, and would have been much more so but for the inclement state of the weather." "

The report also gives particulars as to the scoring, &c., during the season which has already heen given in our columns. With regard to "A" team, Mr. Warren reports that the; first team have been compelled to make more calls upon the "A" team for many years past, but lam pleased to say that the men called upon in most cases have proved to be very efficient, and are likely to do good service it the first team for years to come. The promotions naturally weakened the "A " team but several new and promising players have been found to fill the places of the promoted players and it is expected that the team will be competent to maintain its position as the Champion "A "team of the County." The second team has played 20 matches, won 14, lost 4, and drawn 2. The scoring shows that there have been A goals for, 4 against ; 36 tries for, 11 against ; 52, minors for, 14 against.—The report was adopted unanimously.

THE TREASURER'S REPORT. The Hon. Treasurer (Mr. T. Pemberton) in his report stated that "The sports held last August were not so great a success as in the previous year owing to the wretched weather which prevailed at the time of opening.. The Committee had made special efforts to induce competition by increasing the amount of prize money and by advertising. The profit was £27 15s. 9id., against £52 us. Bd. in 1891" The accounts show that the principal payments were £l4l 18s. 7d. for railway fares ; £l4O Os. 11d., for dinners, refreshments to players, hotel expenses, visit- ing teams and committee ; £95 is. 3d., insurance of three teams, fee to Medical Association, and amoant paid to injured players. The largest item on the " receipts " side were £658 3s. 41c1., for first team gate money, £127 ss. 4d., " A " team gate money, and £l2O 14s. 6d. subscriptions. The total receipts including a balance from the previous year £54 111 s. 3d. was £1,006 is. 7d.—This report wait also adopted un- animously, after Mr. Dixon had commented upon the growth both of the income and expenditure of the club as compared with the season 1884-5.
GRATUITY TO AN AUDITOR.
Mr. T. WRIGHT moved, and Mr. T. BOWBRS seconded, a motion that Mr. T. Wallington be given a gratuity of' £1 ls. mn addition to his usual grant as auditor. The proposal was adopted.
;eIIE SECRETARY AND TREASURER.

Mr. DIXON moved that a gratuity of £l5 each be given to, the Secretary and Treasurer.—Mr. Bibby seconded this proposal.—Mr. T. Wright moved, as an ameudment, that the usual amount of £lO be given to each of these ofticers.—Mr. Whitaker seconded the amendment.—Mr. Rowe and the Chairman (Mr. Dinwiddie) supported the original proposal, which, was carried by a large majority.
IiNOPPOSED RE-ELECTIONS.

The following officers were re-elected without opposi- tion :--Secretary, Mr. .J. E. Warren ; treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton ; first team reporter, Mr. G. Archer; " A " team reporter, Mr. F. Howard ; " A "team umpire, Mr. T. Boyle ; second team umpire, Mr. J. Smith.

THE ELECTION OF PRESIDENT. There were three nominations for president, namely, Councillor Tinsley, Mr. P. Davies, and Mr. W. Pierpoint. On a vote being taken, it was stated that Mr. Davies was at the top of the list, but he had not obtained a majority over the other two candidates, as was neces- sary according to the rules. However, Mr. Tinsley, who was next on the list, expressed a strong- desire to retire, and ultimately Mr. Davies was declared elected.

div.head: ELECTION OF OTHER OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OTHER OFFICERS.

The following are the names of the officers elected : Captain first team, Mr. H. Ashton ; captain " A" team, Mr. T. Davies; captain second team, Mr. H. Rowe; sub- captain first team, Mr. John I'. Bate; sub-captain " A " team, Mr. W. Antrebus ; umpire first team, Mr. Mr. W. Povey ; auditors Mr. T. Wallington and Mr. W. Webster. The following committee was elected : Messrs. W. Hewitt, T. Bowers, T. Barnes, junr. G. Smith, J. Evans, W. Speakman, G. Gilbert, and J. Jolley. At the conclusion of the business, a vote of thanks to the Chairman was moved by Mr. D. Thmion, and seconded by Mr. W. Pierpoint. Mr. Pierpoint referred to the efforts which he and Mr. Evans had made 25 or 30 years ago to make Warrington an athletic town, and said he thought the seeds then sown had now borne fruit, as athletics now flouriched in Warrington in proportion to its population almost more than in any other town in the kingdom. The vote of thanks was passed and the meet in then terminated.

CRICKET.
Lancashire beat Sussex by 112 ; Notts, 187 ; Maude- bone, 76 for four; gentlemen beat Oxford by ten wickets. BRUTAL TREATMENT OF AN IRISH FARMER.

The Athloae correspondent of the "Dublin Express" states that James Flynn, farmer, who some time ago bid for the grazing 3n a vacant farm, has died from brutal Injuries. On the information of Flynn's daughters, three arrests have been made. THE CONVICT DEEMING.

Deeming has received letters from his relatives in England urging him to make a clear confession of his crime, and so atone as much as possible for the errors of his life. He was deeply affected When he read them, and said to his guard," I hope they will remember me without bitterness when I am gone." DATE OF THE DISSOLUTION.

The Exchange Telegraph Company has high authority for stating that at yesterday's Cabinet Council Ministers decided that subject to alteration arising out of unfore- seen circumstances, the dissolution shall take plaee at the end of June, probably the 20th of that month. . . . . .
The" Central kews "rnis authorised to contradict the above statement.
THE MYSTERIOUS MURDERS IN AMERICA. ANOTHER WOMAN SHOT.

NEW YORK,FRIDAY.—A telegtiam from Denison,Texas, where the extraordinary series of murders occurred yesterday, reports this morning that a fifth woman who lived in one of the houses previously mentioned, was struck by a bullet and wounded, but only slightly. The excitement in the town about the whole affair knows no bound.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
THE ROYAL ASSENT.

The Houses of Parliament met yesterday morning at a quarter-past ten, for the purpose of the Royal assent being given to forty Bills, including the Poor Law (Ire- land) Amendment Act, the Hares Bill, the Gaming Act Amendment Sill, and the Short Titles Bill. The Lords Commissioners were—the Lord Chancellor, Earl Coven- try, and Earl Limerick. Mr. Bartley and Mr. E. Holden, in addition to the Speaker, were the only members of tho House of Commons in attendance. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
AFTERNOON SITTING. The Speaker took the chair at two o'clock, when the House resumed.
THE TERRIBLE DISASTER IN THE MAURITIUS , GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

Baron H. De WORMS, answering Mr. H. S. Wright, read the following telegram from the Acting-Governor to Mauritius to the Secretary for the Col3nies, received at the Colonial Office to-day :—Hurricane devastated Mauritius April 29. One-third Port Louis destroyed. Royal College, 24 churches and chapels, and many sugar mills in country completely wrecked. Over 600 deaths n the country. Over one thousand wounded in Port Louis. District returns incomplete; probably same amount. No loss among the military. Estimated re- duction of crop one half, destruction 'to property enormous. No famine apprehended. All relief measures taken. Panic allayed, order and quiet reign, but in presence of thousand homeless people pecuniary assits- ance urgently needed." THE CLERGY DISCIPLINE DILL.-Mr. Balfour moved the resolution of which he gave notice yesterday, em- powering the Cemmittee which is now considering the Clergy Discipline Bill to sit continuously, if found de- sirable, until that measure be disposed of.

Mr. Lloyd George moved an amendtnent making the resolution general, and not one applying merely to the Clergy Discipline Dill. The House divided :—For the amendment 40, against 201; majority against 161. The motion was agreed to. The LOCAL GOVERNMENT BILL.— Mr. MacCartney resumed the debate in the second reading of the Irish Local Government Bill. 1 A COUNT OUT.
The House resumed at 9 o'clock. A count was imme- diately moved and only 27 membora being present, the House adjourned.
THE SHIT' CANAL AND WARRING/TON.

The new Bill of the Manchester Ship Canal Coy. was down for hearing before a committee of the House of Lords this week, the committee consisting of the Earl of Ducie (chairman) Viscount Power- court, Lord Wimbourne, and Lord de Vesca. It will be remembered that when this Bill was first issued the Warrington Corporation fotind it neces- sary to take steps for protecting the interests of the town in :regard to the carrying out of some of the projected works in the neighbourhood of Warrington, and in the main the require- ments of the Corporation were conceded. We understand that the Company have now under- taken to complete the lock at Walton so as to en- able vessels to get out of the River Mersey into the canal, and to complete the entrance to the 1% arcing- ton Dock by the time any portion of the Canal between Runcorn Bridge and Latchford is open for traffic. This will enable the Warrington traders to use the Canal as soon as anyone, so far as this section is concerned. With regard to the dock We believe that the Company are prepared to undertake that it shall be completed within three years after the Canal from Eastham to Latchford is open for traffic. This it will be remembered, is what the Company agreed to do in the Act of 1885.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. —The anniversary services in connection with the above Sunday School were held on Sunday, at the Chapel. The sermons, both afternoon and evening, were preached by Councillor J. Jones, ex-skeriff of Chester. Special hymns were creditably rendered by the choir and scholars. There were good congregations. DRUNKENNESS ON LICENSED PREIIISES.—Thos. Fleming, landlord of the Anchor Inn, Lymm, was charged with permitting drunkenness on his premises on the 20th of April, and E. Gilbert was charged with being drunk on the premises on the occasion.—Fleming was dismissed, and Gilbert was fined 53.

CARRYING GUNS WITHOUT LICEITCR.—WiIIiam Perkins, Alexander Mclntyre, and John Blackledge were charged with carrying guns without a license on the 2nd of March. The Bench dismissed the case of 13Iackledge, fined Perkins 10s. and costs, and mulcted Mclntyre in the costs.

LYMM ARMY CAPTAIN AND HIS DOG : HEAVY PENALTY FOR DEFYING THE COIIIIT.-At the Lymm , Petty Sessions, yesterday, Captain !Eric Manion, of Lymm, who did not appear, summoned on a charge of disobeying a recent order of the ccurt to destroy a savage dog. Mr. A. Browne defended. Police-Sergeant Griffiths deposed that he went to the Orford Barracks, Warrington, on the 7th inst., where the defendant was stationed, and saw the dog there alive.—Mr. Lister said this was an absolute contempt of court. It was a matter of great surprise that a gentleman of Captain Manson's position, hold- ing nor Majesty's commission, could treat an order of the court with contempt. They could not allow Captain Manson to treat a ci vu l court in this way. It was entirely a question of who should be the stronger of the two, Captain Manson or the court. The Bench fined the defendant £1 perday for 16 days during which the order of the court had remained unexecuted and the costs, in default of payment distress to be levied on the defendant, or in default he to go to prison for two months.
